5	config schema — is [README.md](README.md). This file is what a session **here** has to get right.
6	
7	## Configuring the fleet
8	
9	- **Keeping a repo out of the fleet** — add its full `owner/name` to `exclude` on this pack's
10	  config entry. Nothing else opts a repo out: an archived or forked repo is reported as out of scope
11	  but still walked, and a repo that simply never adopted is `uncovered`, which is a finding rather
12	  than a choice. If a repo should not be measured, say so in `exclude` and the reports stop asking
13	  about it.
14	
15	- **Adding or changing a `packSeeds` entry** — get it right *before* the sweep next runs. The
16	  sweep seeds and never overrides, so a wrong seed reaches each member exactly once and then sticks;
17	  correcting it here un-writes nothing, and undoing it is a change in every member's repo. Land the
18	  entry and its own declaration together, then read the next run's report rather than assuming.
19	
20	- **Declaring a pack this fleet also seeds** — write the same config in both places, spelling
21	  every default out on both sides rather than leaving one implicit. `seeds-agree` compares them
22	  literally, because nothing in this pack may know what one pack's absent key means. A pack the
23	  fleet standardizes on but this repo does not itself run has nothing to agree with, and is fine.
24	
25	## Acting on what a sweep reports
26	
27	- **Acting on an `add-packs` work-list issue** — the work is a declaration and a reviewed PR **in
28	  the named member**, never here. A session in this repo is scoped to this repo, so if every item
29	  names another repo there is nothing here to do: say the scope is the blocker rather than writing
30	  to the issues, which are the only thing within reach and are not the work.
31	
32	- **Acting on a scanned pack suggestion** — it is a recommendation, never a verdict.
33	  A fingerprint is a way to *suspect* a pack is wanted; whether to declare it is the member's call,
34	  and closing the issue `not planned` is a standing answer the scan honours rather than re-opening.
35	  A **forced** addition is the other thing entirely — a decision already made — so adopt what
36	  its issue says instead of re-judging whether it was wanted.
37	
38	- **Reading `unknown` in a report** — it means the sweep could not look, not that it looked and
39	  found nothing. Never convert one into a verdict: a repo whose declaration could not be read is
40	  neither covered nor uncovered, an undecided fingerprint is not a non-match, and a member the
41	  pack-seed sweep could not reach is not converged. Fix the access and re-run.
42	
43	- **Judging whether a member is behind** — compare `engineVersion` and `packVersions` against
44	  canon, never the age of its stamped `ref`. The update flows deliberately never rewrite `ref` or
45	  `updated`, so the stamp is provenance — which commit first vendored the mount — and stays
46	  frozen on a member that is perfectly current. Its age measures nothing, and measuring it
47	  calls the whole fleet behind on one arbitrary day.
48	
49	- **Answering why the fleet did not move** — read the member's own artifacts first: its
50	  declaration, its stamp, the runs on its head sha. This repo dispatches; each member converges
51	  itself, with its own token and its own delivery policy. Propose a settings change as a conclusion,
52	  never as the diagnosis.
53	
54	## Running the manual levers
55	
56	- **Pushing canon to the whole fleet now** — create the work item, from a checkout of this repo:
57	
58	  ```
59	  node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-tasks/queue/create-work-item.mjs claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/fleet-baseline
60	  ```
61	
62	  Add `--context "REPOS=owner/a owner/b"` to narrow it (space-separated: a Context line splits on
63	  commas), `--context "DRY_RUN=true"` to see the list without dispatching, or
64	  `--context "INCLUDE_DORMANT=true"` to reach members that stopped their own scheduler on purpose.
65	  Both knobs are read from the item's Context and nowhere else — an item created without them runs
66	  unscoped and live. It queues one run per member and then FOLLOWS each to canon's published engine
67	  and pack versions, reporting per member whether it converged, was already current, or never got
68	  there — never a count of accepted dispatches. A member with nothing to do reads `already-current`,
69	  which is a success, so over-using it is wasteful rather than unsafe.
70	
71	- **Adding a pack across the fleet** — create a `fleet-add-missing-packs` item with
72	  `--context "ADD_PACKS=…"` rather than editing anything. No pack is named anywhere in this pack's
73	  code: every id comes from config or from the item's own Context, which is what keeps the
74	  enforcer from becoming a second place packs are known.
75	
76	## Credentials
77	
78	- **Granting or repairing `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN`** — a fine-grained PAT spanning the owner's
79	  repositories, granted exactly what [`fleet-token.mjs`](fleet-token.mjs)'s table names — the only
80	  place the permissions are written, because a per-sweep subset is always a defensible answer and
81	  never the right one. Grant it whole: the token is granted once, for the pack.
82	
83	- **A sweep reporting `403` or `no-permission`** — the grant is short a permission, which the
84	  error names. It is a grant to fix once, so widen the token rather than re-running: no sweep
85	  retries, because a work list nobody will act on is not a green outcome.

1	# Executable requirements — the framework standard
2	
3	The concrete conventions for running a numbered spec as tests — the mechanics only. The judgment
4	layer they implement — doc-first red-by-default, owner-owned expecteds, honest-gap tracking — is
5	not here, so a new project or a new stack adopts the framework by convention instead of
6	re-deriving it. Worked implementations: GoogleCalendarEventCreator (origin; extension/jsdom
7	rendering), TLDR (adds a cross-tier `server` kind), ShoutsAndWhispers (Flutter port; first `saga`
8	kind).
9	
10	## 1. The layout is the contract
11	
12	- Everything lives under **`dev/requirements/`**: `requirements.md` (the numbered prose spec),
13	  one **top-level folder per kind**, `shared/` for cross-kind infra, and the runners/gates. The
14	  spec file's path is the framework's structural fingerprint — this pack activates on it.
15	- **A requirement line** starts (optionally after a list dash) with a backtick-wrapped dotted
16	  number: `` `4.2` ``. A **leaf** is an id with no finer-numbered child. Parse with one shared
17	  regex (`` ^\s*(?:-\s+)?`(\d+(?:\.\d+)+)` ``) so specs stay drop-in compatible across projects.
18	- **The line is a scannable one-liner; expanded detail collapses.** A leaf in `requirements.md`
19	  reads as a single line the owner skims down the numbered spine on GitHub. Any expansion —
20	  rationale, acceptance notes, edge cases, the owner-verification recipe — lives inside a
21	  collapsed `<details>` block under the line, hidden until the owner expands it. The doc reviews
22	  as a clean spec, not walls of prose; the depth is one click away when wanted, invisible when
23	  not.
24	- **The folder is the kind.** A case's kind is the directory it lives in; the case declares no
25	  kind field. Cases are
26	  `<kind>/cases/<slug>.<leaf-id>.case.<ext>`: a stable feature slug (so retitling a spec section
27	  never forces renames), then the dotted leaf id.
28	- **Artifact expecteds live beside their case** (`<slug>.<id>.png`, `expected/<name>.json`);
29	  failure artifacts (actual/diff renders) go to a gitignored dir, never beside the goldens.
30	- Where the language discovers cases dynamically (Node `require`), the registry walks the
31	  folders; where it cannot (Dart/Flutter), each kind keeps a hand-written `manifest` and **the
32	  gate enforces manifest ⇄ disk equality** — an unregistered case file never runs, so unregistered
33	  must be red.
34	
35	## 2. What the coverage gate checks
36	
37	The bijection gate is one committed test. It must fail on every one of: a leaf no case claims
38	(doc-first red-by-default); a case claiming a non-existent leaf; two cases claiming one leaf; a misnamed case file; a kind directory absent from the registry (or a
39	registered kind with no directory); a manifest out of sync with disk (where manifests exist); an
40	image found in a coded kind's folder (a screenshot cannot verify a gesture or a pure rule); a
41	stray golden no case or step accounts for. Every rule iterates the registry — adding a kind never
42	edits the gate.
43	
44	The gate checks repo state; an interactive feature run also has an *ordering*: after the
45	owner's feature-classified comment, an independent commit updating the spec (no code alongside)
46	precedes the first code commit on the branch. The spec's path defaults to the canonical
47	`dev/requirements/requirements.md`; a project whose spec lives elsewhere (a non-canonical
48	layout, or the pack pulled in via a `requires` from `spec-driven-product`) names it on the pack
49	entry as `config.spec`.
50	
51	## 3. The kind vocabulary
52	
53	Two forces pick a leaf's kind: what can **honestly observe** the assertion, and what gives the
54	**owner the simplest verification**. Prefer the kind whose expected is a **visual the owner checks
55	by sight** — a surface snapshot or a saga storyboard — and whose per-leaf test body is minimal:
56	drive to the state, capture, done, with the golden as the assertion rather than hand-written
57	expectations. Push as many requirements as can honestly be seen onto that visual path — the more
58	of the spec an owner verifies by *looking*, the more of it they actually review. Reserve the coded
59	kinds (behavior, logic) for what an image genuinely cannot see: a gesture's outgoing request, a
60	pure rule. Route each leaf to the kind that can actually see what it asserts:
61	
62	- **surface snapshot** (`popup`, `icon`, `screen`, …): a rendered resting state, pixel-exact
63	  against a committed golden. One golden per leaf, even when several leaves render the same state
64	  — the bijection stays strict.
65	- **behavior**: a driven gesture and its outgoing request/consequence, asserted in code against
66	  the fakes' recordings. No images allowed in the folder.
67	- **logic**: a pure product rule, a coded `verify()` importing shipped code.
68	- **saga** (§4): a multi-step story as a golden storyboard.
69	- **per-project kinds** where the product's value is breadth or crosses tiers: a per-target
70	  `extractor`/`support` kind (one case per supported external target, proven on committed real
71	  samples), a `server` kind (the boundary's half of a two-tier rule, against the real handler).
72	- **heavy/e2e singleton**: "the product loads in the real environment" — one case, its own lane,
73	  never in the default loop.
74	
75	## 4. Sagas: stories as storyboards
76	
77	Single frames prove states; **sagas prove transitions and causality** — what arriving, acting, or
78	time passing *changes*. Use a saga when the requirement is the story ("a message sent before I
79	arrived never appears; one sent after I arrived does"), not decomposable into independent resting
80	states without losing the claim.
81	
82	- A saga case is an ordered list of **steps**; each step = a caption plus an action against the
83	  fake world; after each step the runner captures one golden frame `<slug>.<id>.step-NN.png`.
84	- The **caption narrates the story** in user terms — captions surface in the gallery.
85	- One saga = one leaf; the frames are that one case's expected (all frames pixel-exact, same
86	  ownership rules as any golden). Keep sagas to 3–6 frames; a longer story is usually two sagas.
87	- Saga steps drive the **same real entry point** as every other kind (the shipped app shell/render
88	  function) — a saga must never become a scripted slideshow of hand-arranged states.
89	
90	**Animated saga goldens** (recording the motion, not the frames). A per-step frame proves a resting
91	state; a saga can instead be **one animated golden** — an APNG per leaf — recording the real UI
92	*moving* between steps. What keeps it delay-free and deterministic:
93	
94	- **Strip dead delay, keep the animation.** Render time is virtual, so a scripted wait is a run of
95	  *identical* frames — dedup consecutive identical frames and clamp any single hold, so the golden
96	  holds motion, never waiting (a 3 s wait must not become 3 s of golden).
97	- **Lossless, so byte-identity still holds.** Encode APNG, not GIF (whose palette and dithering
98	  aren't deterministic); the comparison stays exact byte-identity and a mismatch writes a per-frame
99	  `expected | actual | diff` to the gitignored failures dir. Capture at a low DPR — lossless costs
100	  no fidelity for it. Flutter reads each frame off the `RepaintBoundary` via `toImage` inside
101	  `runAsync` (the fake-async test zone won't otherwise complete the byte read).
102	- **Mark the gesture.** Paint an expanding ring at each real pointer gesture over the pre-reaction
103	  frame so the strip shows *where* the user acted; programmatic world changes draw none.
104	
105	## 5. Determinism or it isn't spec
106	
107	A rendered expected is only owner-ownable if it is byte-stable forever:
108	
109	- **Pin the clock.** One shared reference time (`REFERENCE_NOW`) threaded to everything that
110	  formats or compares dates; fixture data is authored relative to it. Never wall-clock.
111	- **Fake every nondeterministic input**: network (map tiles, avatars — deterministic generated
112	  substitutes), randomness, platform sensors, locale (pin it; date copy is locale-sensitive),
113	  viewport (one fixed logical size and pixel ratio).
114	- **Load real fonts** in the render harness — test environments default to a glyph-less stub that
115	  renders text as boxes. Load the product's bundled families plus the
116	  icon font; watch for styles that don't inherit the family (button text styles are the classic
117	  leak) — pin the family there explicitly.

# Executable requirements — the framework standard

The concrete conventions for running a numbered spec as tests — the mechanics only. The judgment
layer they implement — doc-first red-by-default, owner-owned expecteds, honest-gap tracking — is
not here, so a new project or a new stack adopts the framework by convention instead of
re-deriving it. Worked implementations: GoogleCalendarEventCreator (origin; extension/jsdom
rendering), TLDR (adds a cross-tier `server` kind), ShoutsAndWhispers (Flutter port; first `saga`
kind).

## 1. The layout is the contract

- Everything lives under **`dev/requirements/`**: `requirements.md` (the numbered prose spec),
  one **top-level folder per kind**, `shared/` for cross-kind infra, and the runners/gates. The
  spec file's path is the framework's structural fingerprint — this pack activates on it.
- **A requirement line** starts (optionally after a list dash) with a backtick-wrapped dotted
  number: `` `4.2` ``. A **leaf** is an id with no finer-numbered child. Parse with one shared
  regex (`` ^\s*(?:-\s+)?`(\d+(?:\.\d+)+)` ``) so specs stay drop-in compatible across projects.
- **The line is a scannable one-liner; expanded detail collapses.** A leaf in `requirements.md`
  reads as a single line the owner skims down the numbered spine on GitHub. Any expansion —
  rationale, acceptance notes, edge cases, the owner-verification recipe — lives inside a
  collapsed `<details>` block under the line, hidden until the owner expands it. The doc reviews
  as a clean spec, not walls of prose; the depth is one click away when wanted, invisible when
  not.
- **The folder is the kind.** A case's kind is the directory it lives in; the case declares no
  kind field. Cases are
  `<kind>/cases/<slug>.<leaf-id>.case.<ext>`: a stable feature slug (so retitling a spec section
  never forces renames), then the dotted leaf id.
- **Artifact expecteds live beside their case** (`<slug>.<id>.png`, `expected/<name>.json`);
  failure artifacts (actual/diff renders) go to a gitignored dir, never beside the goldens.
- Where the language discovers cases dynamically (Node `require`), the registry walks the
  folders; where it cannot (Dart/Flutter), each kind keeps a hand-written `manifest` and **the
  gate enforces manifest ⇄ disk equality** — an unregistered case file never runs, so unregistered
  must be red.

## 2. What the coverage gate checks

The bijection gate is one committed test. It must fail on every one of: a leaf no case claims
(doc-first red-by-default); a case claiming a non-existent leaf; two cases claiming one leaf; a misnamed case file; a kind directory absent from the registry (or a
registered kind with no directory); a manifest out of sync with disk (where manifests exist); an
image found in a coded kind's folder (a screenshot cannot verify a gesture or a pure rule); a
stray golden no case or step accounts for. Every rule iterates the registry — adding a kind never
edits the gate.

The gate checks repo state; an interactive feature run also has an *ordering*: after the
owner's feature-classified comment, an independent commit updating the spec (no code alongside)
precedes the first code commit on the branch. The spec's path defaults to the canonical
`dev/requirements/requirements.md`; a project whose spec lives elsewhere (a non-canonical
layout, or the pack pulled in via a `requires` from `spec-driven-product`) names it on the pack
entry as `config.spec`.

## 3. The kind vocabulary

Two forces pick a leaf's kind: what can **honestly observe** the assertion, and what gives the
**owner the simplest verification**. Prefer the kind whose expected is a **visual the owner checks
by sight** — a surface snapshot or a saga storyboard — and whose per-leaf test body is minimal:
drive to the state, capture, done, with the golden as the assertion rather than hand-written
expectations. Push as many requirements as can honestly be seen onto that visual path — the more
of the spec an owner verifies by *looking*, the more of it they actually review. Reserve the coded
kinds (behavior, logic) for what an image genuinely cannot see: a gesture's outgoing request, a
pure rule. Route each leaf to the kind that can actually see what it asserts:

- **surface snapshot** (`popup`, `icon`, `screen`, …): a rendered resting state, pixel-exact
  against a committed golden. One golden per leaf, even when several leaves render the same state
  — the bijection stays strict.
- **behavior**: a driven gesture and its outgoing request/consequence, asserted in code against
  the fakes' recordings. No images allowed in the folder.
- **logic**: a pure product rule, a coded `verify()` importing shipped code.
- **saga** (§4): a multi-step story as a golden storyboard.
- **per-project kinds** where the product's value is breadth or crosses tiers: a per-target
  `extractor`/`support` kind (one case per supported external target, proven on committed real
  samples), a `server` kind (the boundary's half of a two-tier rule, against the real handler).
- **heavy/e2e singleton**: "the product loads in the real environment" — one case, its own lane,
  never in the default loop.

## 4. Sagas: stories as storyboards

Single frames prove states; **sagas prove transitions and causality** — what arriving, acting, or
time passing *changes*. Use a saga when the requirement is the story ("a message sent before I
arrived never appears; one sent after I arrived does"), not decomposable into independent resting
states without losing the claim.

- A saga case is an ordered list of **steps**; each step = a caption plus an action against the
  fake world; after each step the runner captures one golden frame `<slug>.<id>.step-NN.png`.
- The **caption narrates the story** in user terms — captions surface in the gallery.
- One saga = one leaf; the frames are that one case's expected (all frames pixel-exact, same
  ownership rules as any golden). Keep sagas to 3–6 frames; a longer story is usually two sagas.
- Saga steps drive the **same real entry point** as every other kind (the shipped app shell/render
  function) — a saga must never become a scripted slideshow of hand-arranged states.

**Animated saga goldens** (recording the motion, not the frames). A per-step frame proves a resting
state; a saga can instead be **one animated golden** — an APNG per leaf — recording the real UI
*moving* between steps. What keeps it delay-free and deterministic:

- **Strip dead delay, keep the animation.** Render time is virtual, so a scripted wait is a run of
  *identical* frames — dedup consecutive identical frames and clamp any single hold, so the golden
  holds motion, never waiting (a 3 s wait must not become 3 s of golden).
- **Lossless, so byte-identity still holds.** Encode APNG, not GIF (whose palette and dithering
  aren't deterministic); the comparison stays exact byte-identity and a mismatch writes a per-frame
  `expected | actual | diff` to the gitignored failures dir. Capture at a low DPR — lossless costs
  no fidelity for it. Flutter reads each frame off the `RepaintBoundary` via `toImage` inside
  `runAsync` (the fake-async test zone won't otherwise complete the byte read).
- **Mark the gesture.** Paint an expanding ring at each real pointer gesture over the pre-reaction
  frame so the strip shows *where* the user acted; programmatic world changes draw none.

## 5. Determinism or it isn't spec

A rendered expected is only owner-ownable if it is byte-stable forever:

- **Pin the clock.** One shared reference time (`REFERENCE_NOW`) threaded to everything that
  formats or compares dates; fixture data is authored relative to it. Never wall-clock.
- **Fake every nondeterministic input**: network (map tiles, avatars — deterministic generated
  substitutes), randomness, platform sensors, locale (pin it; date copy is locale-sensitive),
  viewport (one fixed logical size and pixel ratio).
- **Load real fonts** in the render harness — test environments default to a glyph-less stub that
  renders text as boxes. Load the product's bundled families plus the
  icon font; watch for styles that don't inherit the family (button text styles are the classic
  leak) — pin the family there explicitly.
- **Never wait for "settled".** Indeterminate spinners animate forever; use fixed-duration pumps
  so an in-flight state is a capturable, deterministic frame.

## 6. Rendering recipes per stack

- **Browser-extension / DOM products** (the origin recipe): feed the case's fake data to the real
  `render()` in a jsdom document seeded from the real HTML, fold the real CSS on as inline styles,
  rasterize with satori + resvg, compare with pixelmatch at **zero tolerated diff ratio**. No real
  browser: deterministic and dependency-light, at a documented fidelity tradeoff.
- **Flutter**: widget-test golden files are the native equivalent — pump the real app shell
  against the fake world and `matchesGoldenFile`; `--update-goldens` is the refresh lane. Load
  fonts from the FontManifest (icons included). The fake world (scripted location/auth/backend
  that also *records* what the UI asked) is the product's own testing library so the requirements
  package and unit tests share it.
- Whatever the stack: the comparison is **pixel-exact**. A tolerance is a standing invitation for
  unreviewed drift; if a platform renders unstably, fix the determinism (fonts, clock, fakes), not
  the threshold.

## 7. The gallery is derived output

- The spec doubles as a visual gallery: under every image-kind leaf, machine-managed image lines
  (tagged with an HTML comment marker) embed the committed goldens — saga leaves get their full
  captioned storyboard strip.
- A committed **gallery gate** keeps the doc equal to the generator's output byte-for-byte.
  Regenerate via the tool, never by hand.

## 8. Refresh is a review step

One committed refresh entry point regenerates all goldens **and** the gallery together, so they
cannot skew. Running it is how an *intended* UI change lands — the refreshed PNGs ride the diff
for the owner to approve. It is never how a red case gets fixed: the re-baselining approval
procedure (surface actual/expected/diff, ask, only then re-baseline) is canon in the
writing-tests skill and the spec-driven-product playbook.

3	Portable practices for repos built on Firebase (Auth, Firestore, Cloud Functions, FCM). Earned in
4	missingbulb/ShoutsAndWhispers; keep product-specific schema in the consuming repo's docs.
5	Environment separation — dev/prod projects, App Check, store gating — is not this pack's.
6	
7	## 1. Security rules are merge-aware and default-deny
8	
9	- **End every ruleset with an explicit catch-all deny** and grant per collection; a collection
10	  nobody thought about must be unreachable, not accidentally open.
11	- **Write rules against merge semantics, not just creates.** Clients using `set(merge: true)`
12	  surface the **post-merge** document in `request.resource.data` — a key-presence check that is
13	  right for `create` silently breaks on `update`. For updates, validate
14	  `request.resource.data.diff(resource.data).affectedKeys()` (what the client actually touched);
15	  for creates, validate `keys()`.
16	- **Guard every field dereference for absence.** Distinct writers legitimately upsert disjoint
17	  field subsets of one doc; an unguarded `d.field` on a missing key throws and denies. Pattern:
18	  `!('field' in d) || <validation>`.
19	- **Server-owned fields are absent from the client-allowed key list**, not "checked for equality"
20	  — with `diff().affectedKeys().hasOnly([...])` a client physically cannot touch them (rate-limit
21	  stamps, server-computed aggregates).
22	- **Pin client timestamps to `request.time`** (`FieldValue.serverTimestamp()` satisfies it) on any
23	  write whose freshness matters — but scope the pin to
24	  writes that touch those fields, or unrelated single-field merges get rejected.
25	- **Bound every client-writable string/blob** (length caps in rules); an unbounded field is a
26	  free storage channel.
27	- **Admin-SDK code bypasses rules** — a rules review must enumerate what *functions* write too;
28	  "rules allow it" and "the system writes it" are different lists.
29	
30	## 2. Functions own identity, validation, and limits
31	
32	- **Identity comes from the verified token, never the request body** (`request.auth`,
33	  `token.name`/`picture` claims).
34	- **Validate inputs at the boundary like an adversary wrote them**: type-check, range-check
35	  (`NaN`/`Infinity` slip through naive numeric checks), length-cap, and enum-check before any
36	  read or write; reject with typed `HttpsError`s (`invalid-argument`, `unauthenticated`,
37	  `resource-exhausted`) so clients can react specifically.
38	- **Rate limits need a transaction.** A read-check-write cooldown is bypassable by firing calls
39	  concurrently; run the read + check + stamp inside `runTransaction` so concurrent invocations
40	  serialize. A thrown `HttpsError` inside the transaction aborts it and propagates unchanged.
41	- **Chunk batched writes well under the 500-op limit** and treat multi-batch fan-out as
42	  at-least-once: a mid-sequence crash plus client retry duplicates the early batches. Document
43	  the idempotency-key escape hatch even if v1 doesn't implement it.
44	- **Push is best-effort by construction**: notification failures must never fail the triggering
45	  call; clean up dead tokens on the *actual* error codes
46	  (`messaging/registration-token-not-registered` — verify codes against the installed
47	  firebase-admin, not memory or old blog posts).
48	
49	## 3. Test logic pure, rules empirically
50	
51	- **Extract decision logic into pure modules** (audience selection, filtering, formatting) so the
52	  default suite runs with zero emulators and zero mocks of the Firebase SDK.
53	- **When rules themselves are under test, test them empirically** with
54	  `@firebase/rules-unit-testing` against the real emulator — simulate each *exact client write
55	  shape* the app performs (create vs merge-update vs single-field token write) plus each
56	  forbidden shape.
57	- **Cross-language contracts get mirrored test vectors.** When client and server must compute the
58	  same derived value (a geohash, a normalization), commit identical input→output vectors in both
59	  suites and diff the literals in CI — "both use the standard algorithm" is not a proof.
60	
61	## 4. Deploy layout and aliases
62	
63	- **Keep the Firebase project root self-contained** — the directory holding `firebase.json`, its
64	  `.firebaserc`, rules/indexes, and `functions/`. That root may be the repo root or a dedicated
65	  subfolder (e.g. `firebase/`); the CLI walks up to find `firebase.json` and resolves every path
66	  inside it *relative to that file*, so a subfolder needs no path edits — just run deploys from it
67	  (or pass `--config <dir>/firebase.json`). Keep compiled output (`functions/lib/`) and
68	  `.firebase/` gitignored.
69	- **Commit `.firebaserc` with named aliases and make the default the safe target** (see
70	  the create-release-plan skill for the full environment discipline). Deploy commands in docs always name
71	  what they deploy (`--only functions,firestore`).
72	- **Smoke-load the built entrypoint in the test lane** (`node -e "require('./lib/index.js')"`).
73	  A Node-major skew between build and runtime, or a bad build, surfaces as a module crash the
74	  first time the deployed function is invoked.

1	# Flutter
2	
3	Portable, project-agnostic practices for Flutter / Dart codebases — true for any Flutter project
4	read cold. Earned in missingbulb/ShoutsAndWhispers (a Firebase-backed, location-driven app with an
5	executable-requirements UI suite); keep anything project-specific in the consuming repo's docs.
6	
7	## Architecture: ports out of the widget tree
8	
9	- **Widgets depend on ports, never on plugins.** Every platform/backend concern (location, auth,
10	  push, backend calls, the clock) enters the UI as a hand-written abstract interface with pure-Dart
11	  value types; plugin adapters (`geolocator`, `firebase_*`, `google_sign_in`, …) implement them and
12	  are constructed **only** in `main.dart`. A plugin type leaking into a screen (a geolocator
13	  `Position`, a `FirebaseFunctionsException`) is a defect: it silently couples every widget test to
14	  the plugin's platform channels.
15	- **Enforce the boundary with a committed import-scan test** (dart:io over `lib/ui/`, `lib/screens/`
16	  looking for forbidden import prefixes). The analyzer won't stop a convenient leak.
17	- **Ship the fakes in the package** (`lib/testing/`): scripted fakes for each port that also
18	  *record* what the UI asked of them, plus a `FakeWorld` bundling them with a pinned clock and the
19	  real app shell. Both the app's own tests and any sibling test package (e.g. an
20	  executable-requirements suite) import one fake world — never two parallel ones.
21	- **Extract the root shell into a widget** (`lib/app.dart`) taking the ports as parameters, used
22	  identically by `main.dart` (adapters) and the test harness (fakes). Tests must never rebuild a
23	  parallel MaterialApp — actuals come from the shipped shell.
24	- **Inject the clock.** Any widget that formats or compares times takes a `Clock` port; relative
25	  time rendered from `DateTime.now()` is untestable and drifts goldens.
26	
27	## Widget tests and goldens
28	
29	- **Load real fonts before any golden** — the test binding defaults to the glyph-less Ahem stub
30	  (text renders as boxes). Parse `FontManifest.json` from the root bundle and `FontLoader` every
31	  family (strip the `packages/<pkg>/` prefix so plain family names resolve), which also loads
32	  MaterialIcons; bundle text faces (e.g. Roboto) in the test package's pubspec. Watch for styles
33	  that don't inherit the theme's family — `ButtonStyle`/`styleFrom` text styles are the classic
34	  leak; pin `fontFamily` there explicitly.
35	- **Never `pumpAndSettle` around indeterminate progress indicators** — they schedule frames
36	  forever and the call never returns. Use fixed-duration pumps (`pump()` then
37	  `pump(Duration(...))`); this also makes an in-flight state (a spinner mid-send) a deterministic,
38	  golden-capturable frame. Corollary: after `tap()`, pump **twice** — one frame applies state, the
39	  fixed-duration pump advances implicit animations (ink ripples, color lerps) past the capture.
40	- **Anything that fetches must be injectable**: map tile providers, avatar images. Widget tests
41	  block real HTTP (a 400-returning stub client), so a `NetworkImage`/network `TileProvider` in the
42	  tree means error boxes, not screenshots. Provide a deterministic in-memory substitute (a
43	  canvas-drawn `ImageProvider` works and needs no asset files).
44	- **Fix the viewport per suite**: set `tester.view.physicalSize` and `devicePixelRatio` to one
45	  phone-shaped size (and reset in teardown) so layout — and therefore goldens — can't drift with
46	  the harness default.
47	- **Async lifecycle guards need an epoch counter.** A `start()` that awaits (permission check,
48	  first fix) can re-arm streams/timers after `stop()`/dispose ran mid-await; bump an epoch in
49	  `stop()` and bail after every await if it changed. The symptom (leaked GPS subscription after
50	  sign-out) is invisible in tests that don't await realistically.
51	
52	## Toolchain habits
53	
54	- **Verify plugin APIs against the installed source, not memory.** Major Flutter plugins break
55	  their APIs often (google_sign_in v7's `authenticate()`, flutter_map v7+'s options, geolocator's
56	  settings objects); resolved versions live in the pub cache
57	  (`~/.pub-cache/hosted/pub.dev/<pkg>-<ver>/lib/`) — read them before writing against them.
58	- **`pubspec.lock` moving without `pubspec.yaml` moving is version skew, not a dependency change.**
59	  An app commits its lockfile (only a *library* package gitignores it), so the file is tracked on
60	  purpose — the thing to keep out of the diff is the churn a local `flutter pub get` produces when
61	  the installed SDK resolves differently from CI's. Unless you deliberately ran an upgrade, revert
62	  it: `git checkout -- pubspec.lock`.
63	- **`flutter analyze` at zero issues** (infos included) is the bar a suite holds; lints that fight
64	  a deliberate convention (e.g. `file_names` vs. leaf-id case filenames) get disabled narrowly in
65	  that package's `analysis_options.yaml` with the reason as a comment.
66	- **Sandboxed/CI runners**: `flutter test` can stall for minutes at teardown on GPU-less containers
67	  with dropped sockets. The pattern that holds: stream output, kill the process group the moment
68	  the definitive marker prints (`All tests passed!` / `Some tests failed`), watchdog-kill on output
69	  silence. On healthy machines plain `flutter test` is equivalent — keep the wrapper thin.
70	- **The web sandbox ships no Flutter SDK.** Claude Code on the web boots without Flutter, so tests,
71	  `flutter analyze`, and golden regen can't run until it's installed. Install belongs in the
72	  environment **image** (built once, snapshotted, reused) — never a per-session hook that reinstalls
73	  every start. This pack declares that need in its `env` block ([pack.mjs](pack.mjs)); a project pastes
74	  one generic `environment-setup-command.sh` that runs every active pack's requirement via
75	  [engine/pack_loader/env-requirements.mjs](../../engine/pack_loader/env-requirements.mjs) and asserts it at session start (see [bootstrap.md](../../bootstrap.md)
76	  Part 9).
77

## Architecture: ports out of the widget tree

- **Widgets depend on ports, never on plugins.** Every platform/backend concern (location, auth,
  push, backend calls, the clock) enters the UI as a hand-written abstract interface with pure-Dart
  value types; plugin adapters (`geolocator`, `firebase_*`, `google_sign_in`, …) implement them and
  are constructed **only** in `main.dart`. A plugin type leaking into a screen (a geolocator
  `Position`, a `FirebaseFunctionsException`) is a defect: it silently couples every widget test to
  the plugin's platform channels.
- **Enforce the boundary with a committed import-scan test** (dart:io over `lib/ui/`, `lib/screens/`
  looking for forbidden import prefixes). The analyzer won't stop a convenient leak.
- **Ship the fakes in the package** (`lib/testing/`): scripted fakes for each port that also
  *record* what the UI asked of them, plus a `FakeWorld` bundling them with a pinned clock and the
  real app shell. Both the app's own tests and any sibling test package (e.g. an
  executable-requirements suite) import one fake world — never two parallel ones.
- **Extract the root shell into a widget** (`lib/app.dart`) taking the ports as parameters, used
  identically by `main.dart` (adapters) and the test harness (fakes). Tests must never rebuild a
  parallel MaterialApp — actuals come from the shipped shell.
- **Inject the clock.** Any widget that formats or compares times takes a `Clock` port; relative
  time rendered from `DateTime.now()` is untestable and drifts goldens.

## Widget tests and goldens

- **Load real fonts before any golden** — the test binding defaults to the glyph-less Ahem stub
  (text renders as boxes). Parse `FontManifest.json` from the root bundle and `FontLoader` every
  family (strip the `packages/<pkg>/` prefix so plain family names resolve), which also loads
  MaterialIcons; bundle text faces (e.g. Roboto) in the test package's pubspec. Watch for styles
  that don't inherit the theme's family — `ButtonStyle`/`styleFrom` text styles are the classic
  leak; pin `fontFamily` there explicitly.
- **Never `pumpAndSettle` around indeterminate progress indicators** — they schedule frames
  forever and the call never returns. Use fixed-duration pumps (`pump()` then
  `pump(Duration(...))`); this also makes an in-flight state (a spinner mid-send) a deterministic,
  golden-capturable frame. Corollary: after `tap()`, pump **twice** — one frame applies state, the
  fixed-duration pump advances implicit animations (ink ripples, color lerps) past the capture.
- **Anything that fetches must be injectable**: map tile providers, avatar images. Widget tests
  block real HTTP (a 400-returning stub client), so a `NetworkImage`/network `TileProvider` in the
  tree means error boxes, not screenshots. Provide a deterministic in-memory substitute (a
  canvas-drawn `ImageProvider` works and needs no asset files).
- **Fix the viewport per suite**: set `tester.view.physicalSize` and `devicePixelRatio` to one
  phone-shaped size (and reset in teardown) so layout — and therefore goldens — can't drift with
  the harness default.
- **Async lifecycle guards need an epoch counter.** A `start()` that awaits (permission check,
  first fix) can re-arm streams/timers after `stop()`/dispose ran mid-await; bump an epoch in
  `stop()` and bail after every await if it changed. The symptom (leaked GPS subscription after
  sign-out) is invisible in tests that don't await realistically.

## Toolchain habits

- **Verify plugin APIs against the installed source, not memory.** Major Flutter plugins break
  their APIs often (google_sign_in v7's `authenticate()`, flutter_map v7+'s options, geolocator's
  settings objects); resolved versions live in the pub cache
  (`~/.pub-cache/hosted/pub.dev/<pkg>-<ver>/lib/`) — read them before writing against them.
- **`pubspec.lock` moving without `pubspec.yaml` moving is version skew, not a dependency change.**
  An app commits its lockfile (only a *library* package gitignores it), so the file is tracked on
  purpose — the thing to keep out of the diff is the churn a local `flutter pub get` produces when
  the installed SDK resolves differently from CI's. Unless you deliberately ran an upgrade, revert
  it: `git checkout -- pubspec.lock`.
- **`flutter analyze` at zero issues** (infos included) is the bar a suite holds; lints that fight
  a deliberate convention (e.g. `file_names` vs. leaf-id case filenames) get disabled narrowly in
  that package's `analysis_options.yaml` with the reason as a comment.
- **Sandboxed/CI runners**: `flutter test` can stall for minutes at teardown on GPU-less containers
  with dropped sockets. The pattern that holds: stream output, kill the process group the moment
  the definitive marker prints (`All tests passed!` / `Some tests failed`), watchdog-kill on output
  silence. On healthy machines plain `flutter test` is equivalent — keep the wrapper thin.
- **The web sandbox ships no Flutter SDK.** Claude Code on the web boots without Flutter, so tests,
  `flutter analyze`, and golden regen can't run until it's installed. Install belongs in the
  environment **image** (built once, snapshotted, reused) — never a per-session hook that reinstalls
  every start. This pack declares that need in its `env` block ([pack.mjs](pack.mjs)); a project pastes
  one generic `environment-setup-command.sh` that runs every active pack's requirement via
  [engine/pack_loader/env-requirements.mjs](../../engine/pack_loader/env-requirements.mjs) and asserts it at session start (see [bootstrap.md](../../bootstrap.md)
  Part 9).

Reserve "test it after it's deployed" for behavior you've verified genuinely can't be observed now. - **Make that console request a snippet, not an essay.** Send exactly one code block to paste into the console and ask the user to paste its output back. Skip the prose explaining what you're hoping to learn.

1	# Leaflet
2	
3	Portable, project-agnostic gotchas for the [Leaflet](https://leafletjs.com/) web-mapping library — loading it from a CDN, embedding a map in a page, and the marker/`divIcon` and plugin behaviours that bite regardless of which app renders the map. True for any Leaflet map read cold.
4	
5	- **Feature-detect an optional Leaflet plugin before using it, and fall back to core when its CDN script didn't load.** A plugin's separate `<script>` (markercluster, heat, draw, …) can silently fail to load while the base Leaflet bundle succeeds, leaving `L.markerClusterGroup` (etc.) undefined. Guard the call with `typeof L.markerClusterGroup === "function"` and add markers straight to the map when it's absent — the base map must still render.
6	
7	- **Default an embedded, mid-page map to `scrollWheelZoom: false` so it doesn't hijack the page scroll.** Construct it with `L.map(el, { scrollWheelZoom: false })`, or gate wheel-zoom behind a click/focus.
8	
9	- **Keep the tile provider's attribution — it's a licence term, not decoration.** The `attribution: '… © OpenStreetMap contributors'` on the `L.tileLayer(...)` must stay even when tidying the UI. Set `maxZoom` to the provider's real ceiling (OSM tiles top out at 19) so Leaflet doesn't request zoom levels the provider doesn't serve.
10	
11	- **When a marker needs its own CSS `transform`, put it on an inner element, not the `divIcon` root.** Leaflet positions every marker by writing an inline `transform: translate3d(...)` onto the icon's root element, clobbering any `transform` you set there on the next reposition. Make the icon root a zero-size anchor (`iconSize: [0, 0]`, `iconAnchor: [0, 0]`) and apply your rotation/centring transform to a `<span>` inside its `html`.
12

# Leaflet

Portable, project-agnostic gotchas for the [Leaflet](https://leafletjs.com/) web-mapping library — loading it from a CDN, embedding a map in a page, and the marker/`divIcon` and plugin behaviours that bite regardless of which app renders the map. True for any Leaflet map read cold.

- **Feature-detect an optional Leaflet plugin before using it, and fall back to core when its CDN script didn't load.** A plugin's separate `<script>` (markercluster, heat, draw, …) can silently fail to load while the base Leaflet bundle succeeds, leaving `L.markerClusterGroup` (etc.) undefined. Guard the call with `typeof L.markerClusterGroup === "function"` and add markers straight to the map when it's absent — the base map must still render.

- **Default an embedded, mid-page map to `scrollWheelZoom: false` so it doesn't hijack the page scroll.** Construct it with `L.map(el, { scrollWheelZoom: false })`, or gate wheel-zoom behind a click/focus.

- **Keep the tile provider's attribution — it's a licence term, not decoration.** The `attribution: '… © OpenStreetMap contributors'` on the `L.tileLayer(...)` must stay even when tidying the UI. Set `maxZoom` to the provider's real ceiling (OSM tiles top out at 19) so Leaflet doesn't request zoom levels the provider doesn't serve.

- **When a marker needs its own CSS `transform`, put it on an inner element, not the `divIcon` root.** Leaflet positions every marker by writing an inline `transform: translate3d(...)` onto the icon's root element, clobbering any `transform` you set there on the next reposition. Make the icon root a zero-size anchor (`iconSize: [0, 0]`, `iconAnchor: [0, 0]`) and apply your rotation/centring transform to a `<span>` inside its `html`.

1	# macOS
2	
3	Portable practices for a **native macOS app** — the ones that are true whatever the app does:
4	assembling the app bundle, the TCC and Hardened Runtime pair, the Developer ID → notarization →
5	DMG lane, and the process-lifecycle facts a Mac app cannot get wrong. A default to adapt, not a
6	contract.
7	
8	Distilled from a fleet project shipping a menu-bar agent app built with SwiftPM and published as a
9	notarized DMG. Mac App Store submission is a different track — see `app-store-release`; an iPhone
10	target is `ios`.
11	
12	## The app bundle is assembled, not built
13	
14	- **SwiftPM builds a binary; nothing builds you a `.app`.** `swift build -c release` yields an
15	  executable — the bundle (`Contents/MacOS/<exe>`, `Contents/Info.plist`,
16	  `Contents/Resources/`) is assembled by your own script. Keep that script the single place the
17	  bundle's shape is defined, so the local build and CI produce byte-identical layouts.
18	- **Commit one high-resolution icon master and generate the `.icns`** in the build script (`sips`
19	  to each size into an `.iconset`, then `iconutil -c icns`). Both tools ship with macOS, so the
20	  repo carries one PNG instead of ten, and the icon can't half-update.
21	- **A menu-bar-only app is `LSUIElement: true`** in `Info.plist` — that, not code, is what removes
22	  the Dock icon and the main window.
23	- **Pin `LSMinimumSystemVersion` to the same OS version the package's `platforms:` declares.** They
24	  are two independent claims about the same floor, and only one of them is enforced at launch.
25	
26	## TCC and the Hardened Runtime are two different gates — know which applies
27	
28	Every protected resource needs a **usage-description string** in `Info.plist` (the text of the
29	consent prompt; without it the app is killed rather than prompted) — one key per resource, and they
30	are separate keys for capabilities that feel like one feature: `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` covers
31	audio input, `NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription` covers the Speech framework, and an app that
32	listens *and* transcribes needs both or is killed at whichever it forgot. What each string says is
33	what the user consents to. Only *some* resources also need a **codesign entitlement**, and only
34	under the Hardened Runtime:
35	
36	- **Notarization requires the Hardened Runtime** (`codesign --options runtime`), and under it a
37	  resource-access exception must be granted explicitly by entitlement — device capture
38	  (`com.apple.security.device.audio-input`, camera) is the classic one. So **turning on
39	  notarization can silently break a capability an ad-hoc build had**, because the ad-hoc build was
40	  never running under the restriction. Ship the entitlement in the same change as the runtime flag.
41	- **Capabilities gated purely by TCC plus their usage string need no entitlement at all** (speech
42	  recognition is the worked example). Adding one you don't need is noise; omitting one you do need
43	  is a runtime failure no build step catches.
44	- **Do not enable the App Sandbox on the Developer ID track.** The sandbox belongs to the Mac App
45	  Store lane, needs a different (Apple Distribution) certificate, and silently removes
46	  capabilities the direct-download build has — distributed notifications, for one.
47	
48	## Speech recognition leaves the machine unless you say it must not
49	
50	- **`SFSpeechRecognizer` streams audio to Apple's servers by default.** On-device recognition is
51	  opt-in, and the opt-in is a property of the **request**
52	  (`request.requiresOnDeviceRecognition = true`), not of the recognizer — so it has to be set on
53	  every request the app builds, and a new call site added later starts out server-side. Nothing in
54	  the build says which mode ran; the difference is only visible in what left the machine.
55	- **The opt-in is only honourable where the locale's model is installed.** `supportsOnDeviceRecognition`
56	  is per-recognizer and false until then, and requiring on-device recognition where it isn't
57	  supported fails the request rather than quietly falling back — so check it and decide the degrade
58	  deliberately (refuse the feature, or say plainly that this locale would transcribe off-device).
59	- Speech is TCC-gated, so it needs its usage string and **no** entitlement — see the section above.
60	
61	## Keep signing and notarization an optional, secret-gated lane
62	
63	- **The unsigned path must stay a working path.** Gate the Developer ID + notarization steps on the
64	  signing secrets being present, and ship an **ad-hoc-signed** artifact when they aren't. Make
65	  signing a required step and every fork, and every build in a repo whose secrets aren't set, goes
66	  red for a reason unrelated to the change.
67	- **An ad-hoc signature cannot be notarized.** They are separate lanes, not degrees of the same
68	  one: only an identity-signed bundle can be submitted to the notary service. Don't write a
69	  pipeline that "tries" to notarize whatever it just signed.
70	- **Notarize the distributed container, then staple it** (`notarytool submit --wait`, then `stapler
71	  staple` and `stapler validate`). Stapling is what makes the download open offline without a
72	  round-trip to Apple; skipping it works on your machine and fails on a user's.
73	- **In CI, an imported identity must be in the searchable keychain list.** Creating an ephemeral
74	  keychain, importing the `.p12` and setting the key partition list is not enough —
75	  `codesign` searches the *user's keychain list*, so the new keychain has to be added to it or the
76	  identity is simply not found.
77	- **Say out loud, in a build annotation, which lane ran.** "No signing secret — publishing an
78	  ad-hoc build" turns a silently-degraded artifact into a visible one.
79	
80	## Distribution and the Gatekeeper story you owe the user
81	
82	- **A drag-to-install DMG is a staged folder, not Finder scripting.** Stage the `.app` beside a
83	  symlink to `/Applications`, drop the icon in as `.VolumeIcon.icns`, flag the folder as having a
84	  custom icon, and let `hdiutil create` carry it through. Anything that automates Finder to lay out
85	  the window is fragile in CI and unnecessary.
86	- **Write the Gatekeeper bypass for the OS your users are on.** macOS 15 removed the
87	  right-click → *Open* bypass; the current path is System Settings → Privacy & Security →
88	  *Open Anyway*, or `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine <app>`. An install doc that still says
89	  right-click → Open reads as broken software.
90	- **A notarized build should need none of that** — if your README's manual-bypass section is the
91	  one users actually follow, the signing lane isn't running.
92	
93	## Assume the user's Mac has no developer toolchain
94	
95	The machine running a distributed app installed the artifact; it has no Xcode. Two consequences:
96	
97	- **Diagnostics belong inside the shipped app**, or in a script using only what ships with macOS.
98	  Anything requiring a compiler on the user's machine is a diagnostic that will never be run.
99	- **`command -v swift` does not test for a Swift toolchain.** `/usr/bin/swift` exists on every Mac
100	  as a stub that pops the *"install the command line developer tools?"* dialog when invoked — so
101	  the probe passes and the script asks the user to install several gigabytes of Xcode. Gate on
102	  `xcode-select -p >/dev/null 2>&1`, which fails quietly when the tools are absent.
103	
104	## Exit paths: `applicationWillTerminate` is not "every exit"
105	
106	- **`NSApplication` installs no signal handlers.** `NSApp.terminate` (menu Quit, ⌘Q, the
107	  logout/shutdown Apple Event) runs `applicationWillTerminate`; a bare `SIGTERM` (Activity
108	  Monitor's Quit, `killall`), `SIGINT` or `SIGHUP` kills the process with **no** teardown. Route
109	  them through a `DispatchSourceSignal` into `NSApp.terminate` — and set `signal(sig, SIG_IGN)`
110	  **before** `resume()`, or a signal arriving in the gap still takes the fatal default.
111	  `SIGKILL`, Force Quit and a crash stay uncoverable; name that as residual risk rather than
112	  claiming coverage.
113	- **An uncaught Objective-C exception is an exit path too.** It aborts the process, so no teardown
114	  runs; a framework call that *raises* (rather than throws) is therefore a resource-release bug as
115	  well as a crash. Swift cannot catch `NSException` — a tiny Objective-C target of your own is the
116	  only trap, and it is only safe around calls that validate before mutating.
117	
118	## Sleep, wake, and deferred work
119	
120	- **There is no "the machine is back" notification.** `NSWorkspace.didWakeNotification` also fires
121	  for a dark/Power-Nap wake with nobody there. Fan in the several signals that a real return emits
122	  (wake, screens wake, session became active, the screen-unlocked distributed notification) and
123	  **coalesce them** — a genuine return fires a burst, and each must not schedule its own work.
124	- **Coalesce with an id, not a boolean.** A single `pending` flag deadlocks: something invalidates
125	  the timer, the timer clears the flag, and whichever ordering loses leaves the next wake either
126	  unable to schedule or double-scheduling. Hold the in-flight work's id; a stale timer compares its
127	  captured id and returns.
128	- **`asyncAfter` work scheduled before sleep fires immediately on wake.** Give every intentional
129	  stop a generation counter, capture the generation when scheduling, and abort in the closure if it
130	  moved — otherwise deferred work reacquires resources on the way *into* sleep or before the
131	  machine has settled. When cancelling in-flight work, reset the latches beside it too, or they
132	  stay stuck and block everything after.
133	- **Measure a span that includes a sleep with `Date()`, not `ProcessInfo.systemUptime`.** The
134	  monotonic clock does not advance while the machine sleeps — which is exactly the span you are
135	  trying to measure. Use `systemUptime` for the opposite question ("how long, while we were
136	  awake").
137	
138	## Holding a device the user can unplug
139	
140	If the app captures from shared hardware (microphone, camera), these are the rules that cost the
141	most to learn:
142	
143	- **Release the device on every path where capture ends.** A process that dies with its IO proc
144	  still registered can leave some USB devices wedged until physically re-plugged. This is necessary
145	  and *not sufficient* — a device can also wedge below the user-space audio daemon, where no
146	  teardown of yours helps.
147	- **Never construct a capture engine to ask whether a device exists.** Materializing an input node
148	  opens the default device and mints a hidden per-client aggregate device; a retry ladder built on
149	  that is not a cheap probe but an open/close plus an aggregate create-and-destroy, repeated for as
150	  long as the hardware is missing. Query the HAL's device properties instead — a property read
151	  opens nothing and can be sampled forever for free. The churn is observable rather than
152	  theoretical: each hidden aggregate appears in the HAL as `CADefaultDeviceAggregate-<pid>-<n>`, so
153	  what a retry ladder is really doing can be counted instead of argued about.
154	- **Presence is not usability, at either layer.** Mid-teardown a device enumerates as alive with an
155	  unreadable name and a **zero** sample rate. Require a nonzero rate and a sane channel count, and
156	  judge the *system default* input — a healthy device behind a broken default is not one you can
157	  capture from. One layer up, the engine lies in the opposite direction: with the input torn down,
158	  the input node's `outputFormat(forBus: 0)` still reports a plausible 48 kHz while its
159	  `inputFormat` reports 0, so a guard written against the wrong one waves through starts that
160	  cannot succeed — read both and require them to agree. Whatever a new probe reads, ask what that
161	  field says while the device is absent.
162	- **A duration is a claim about a span you observed.** "It has been present for N seconds" is only
163	  as good as the observation behind it: a state maintained by a timer must be **seeded at start**
164	  (a repeating timer does not fire immediately) and **invalidated across any gap** — a sleep is a
165	  gap, and carrying a settle clock straight through one makes the gate inert on exactly the
166	  transition it was built for. Model "not observed" as its own state, distinct from "absent", and
167	  key the span on the device's **UID** — an unplug-and-replug, or a swap for a different mic, is a
168	  new arrival that starts its own clock rather than inheriting the departed device's.
169	- **"Started" is not "working".** A running engine delivering buffers of pure silence looks
170	  identical to a healthy one from the inside. Measure what actually arrives, publish a health state
171	  the UI renders, and when a failure mode has exactly one remedy, name **that** remedy rather than
172	  the generic one.
173	- **Compile-green is not a gate for device code.** `swift build` cannot see a raise-vs-throw bug or
174	  a lifecycle race, and both are reachable in the first second of a run. A change here is not
175	  verified until the app has actually launched on a Mac. Reaching the interesting case needs no
176	  hardware theatre: let the display sleep and `coreaudiod` tears its device contexts down seconds
177	  later, which is the same transition as an unplug from the app's point of view.

  what a retry ladder is really doing can be counted instead of argued about.
- **Presence is not usability, at either layer.** Mid-teardown a device enumerates as alive with an
  unreadable name and a **zero** sample rate. Require a nonzero rate and a sane channel count, and
  judge the *system default* input — a healthy device behind a broken default is not one you can
  capture from. One layer up, the engine lies in the opposite direction: with the input torn down,
  the input node's `outputFormat(forBus: 0)` still reports a plausible 48 kHz while its
  `inputFormat` reports 0, so a guard written against the wrong one waves through starts that
  cannot succeed — read both and require them to agree. Whatever a new probe reads, ask what that
  field says while the device is absent.
- **A duration is a claim about a span you observed.** "It has been present for N seconds" is only
  as good as the observation behind it: a state maintained by a timer must be **seeded at start**
  (a repeating timer does not fire immediately) and **invalidated across any gap** — a sleep is a
  gap, and carrying a settle clock straight through one makes the gate inert on exactly the
  transition it was built for. Model "not observed" as its own state, distinct from "absent", and
  key the span on the device's **UID** — an unplug-and-replug, or a swap for a different mic, is a
  new arrival that starts its own clock rather than inheriting the departed device's.
- **"Started" is not "working".** A running engine delivering buffers of pure silence looks
  identical to a healthy one from the inside. Measure what actually arrives, publish a health state
  the UI renders, and when a failure mode has exactly one remedy, name **that** remedy rather than
  the generic one.
- **Compile-green is not a gate for device code.** `swift build` cannot see a raise-vs-throw bug or
  a lifecycle race, and both are reachable in the first second of a run. A change here is not
  verified until the app has actually launched on a Mac. Reaching the interesting case needs no
  hardware theatre: let the display sleep and `coreaudiod` tears its device contexts down seconds
  later, which is the same transition as an unplug from the app's point of view.

1	# Node.js
2	
3	Portable, project-agnostic practices for working in Node.js / npm codebases — package management, scripts, module resolution, runtime gotchas — true for any Node project read cold.
4	
5	## Module resolution
6	
7	- **A *named* import from a package's CommonJS entry can silently yield `undefined`.** Node recovers named bindings from a CJS module by static analysis, and that analysis fails on plenty of real entry points (a re-export built at runtime, a conditional assignment) — with no error: the import resolves, the binding is `undefined`, and the failure surfaces later as "x is not a function". When a package ships both entries, import the **ESM** one explicitly (`…/package/index.mjs`, or the `import` condition of its `exports`) for named bindings; when it doesn't, `import pkg from '…'` and destructure off the default. Resolve the package's own directory (`$(npm root -g)/<pkg>` for a global install) rather than hardcoding an absolute path into a version-pinned layout, which moves under you on the next image or upgrade.
8	- **Modern Node (22.7+) detects ES-module syntax in a `.js` file on its own** — no `"type": "module"`, no flag, no warning. A directory of ES modules therefore needs **no `package.json` of its own** just to be loadable; adding one to declare module-ness is cargo cult, and one already present for that reason is vestigial. (Prefer `.js` consistently within a tree over mixing in `.mjs` for the same purpose; the extension is then a style choice, not a signal.)
9	
10	## Test discovery
11	
12	- **`node --test` skips dot-directories, so a bare invocation over a suite living under one runs
13	  zero tests and exits green.** Node's default discovery walks the tree but ignores hidden
14	  directories outright, and finding nothing is *success* — a run reporting no failures because it
15	  found no tests reads exactly like a passing suite. Any CI step or local command meant to exercise
16	  tests under a dot-path must pass that path (or an explicit glob) as an argument, and whoever adds
17	  the step confirms it by watching the **test count be non-zero**, never by watching it go green.
18	  Naming a path is not enough — the argument must **resolve to files that exist**: a typo'd
19	  glob, a moved fixture or a renamed directory produces the identical zero-test green, so the
20	  property to assert is that every path a `node --test` invocation names still matches something
21	  in the tree.
22	
23	## jsdom diverges from a real browser in ways a green test can hide
24	
25	Two that recur:
26	
27	- **`body.innerText` is null in jsdom.** Code reading `el.innerText || el.textContent` therefore falls through to `textContent` under test, which *includes* the `<script>` / `<style>` text, `<select>` / `<option>` text, and CSS-hidden text a real browser's `innerText` omits. Treat body-text results as jsdom-optimistic; never add a test that only passes because of it.
28	- **`runScripts: "outside-only"` (the default) parses `<noscript>` into live DOM — the opposite of a real browser.** A `textContent` read looks clean under test but splices the `<noscript>` markup into the value in Chrome, which keeps `<noscript>` as raw text. Parse a script-free fragment with `runScripts: "dangerously"` to reproduce the browser.
29

# Node.js

Portable, project-agnostic practices for working in Node.js / npm codebases — package management, scripts, module resolution, runtime gotchas — true for any Node project read cold.

## Module resolution

- **A *named* import from a package's CommonJS entry can silently yield `undefined`.** Node recovers named bindings from a CJS module by static analysis, and that analysis fails on plenty of real entry points (a re-export built at runtime, a conditional assignment) — with no error: the import resolves, the binding is `undefined`, and the failure surfaces later as "x is not a function". When a package ships both entries, import the **ESM** one explicitly (`…/package/index.mjs`, or the `import` condition of its `exports`) for named bindings; when it doesn't, `import pkg from '…'` and destructure off the default. Resolve the package's own directory (`$(npm root -g)/<pkg>` for a global install) rather than hardcoding an absolute path into a version-pinned layout, which moves under you on the next image or upgrade.
- **Modern Node (22.7+) detects ES-module syntax in a `.js` file on its own** — no `"type": "module"`, no flag, no warning. A directory of ES modules therefore needs **no `package.json` of its own** just to be loadable; adding one to declare module-ness is cargo cult, and one already present for that reason is vestigial. (Prefer `.js` consistently within a tree over mixing in `.mjs` for the same purpose; the extension is then a style choice, not a signal.)

## Test discovery

- **`node --test` skips dot-directories, so a bare invocation over a suite living under one runs
  zero tests and exits green.** Node's default discovery walks the tree but ignores hidden
  directories outright, and finding nothing is *success* — a run reporting no failures because it
  found no tests reads exactly like a passing suite. Any CI step or local command meant to exercise
  tests under a dot-path must pass that path (or an explicit glob) as an argument, and whoever adds
  the step confirms it by watching the **test count be non-zero**, never by watching it go green.
  Naming a path is not enough — the argument must **resolve to files that exist**: a typo'd
  glob, a moved fixture or a renamed directory produces the identical zero-test green, so the
  property to assert is that every path a `node --test` invocation names still matches something
  in the tree.

## jsdom diverges from a real browser in ways a green test can hide

Two that recur:

- **`body.innerText` is null in jsdom.** Code reading `el.innerText || el.textContent` therefore falls through to `textContent` under test, which *includes* the `<script>` / `<style>` text, `<select>` / `<option>` text, and CSS-hidden text a real browser's `innerText` omits. Treat body-text results as jsdom-optimistic; never add a test that only passes because of it.
- **`runScripts: "outside-only"` (the default) parses `<noscript>` into live DOM — the opposite of a real browser.** A `textContent` read looks clean under test but splices the `<noscript>` markup into the value in Chrome, which keeps `<noscript>` as raw text. Parse a script-free fragment with `runScripts: "dangerously"` to reproduce the browser.

1	# product-wiki — the self-growing product research wiki
2	
3	This project keeps its market/user/competitor research as a self-growing wiki
4	under `product-wiki/` (Karpathy's LLM-wiki pattern: compile findings once, refine in
5	place). Layout, required page sections, the Key insights header's shape,
6	growth-log dating, source links, staleness, and the isolation wall are
7	**check-enforced** — the finding is the instruction, so this prose never restates
8	them. The full growth procedure is the pack's task doc
9	(`packs/product-wiki/tasks/wiki-growth/task.md`).
10	
11	- **Every page opens with what it found.** `## Key insights` leads the page: a
12	  few bullets carrying the research's actual conclusions — the numbers, the
13	  competitor that already does this, the thing that turned out not to be true —
14	  enough that a human who reads only the header understands what was researched
15	  and what it means. Not a table of contents ("covers pricing and competitors"),
16	  not a teaser. The body is where the reader goes for evidence, nuance and
17	  citations; the header is where they decide whether they need to.
18	- **Terse, plain, and only the non-obvious.** One short line per bullet, in
19	  ordinary words — no qualifying clause, no citation, no hedge, no jargon a
20	  newcomer would have to decode. Prefer the finding that would *surprise*
21	  someone who knows the field: the thing that turned out not to be true, the
22	  number nobody expects, the competitor who already shipped it. Whether a point
23	  is obvious is genuinely hard to call, so **don't agonise — when in doubt, keep
24	  it**. A borderline-obvious line costs the reader two seconds; a long, careful
25	  line costs them the header.
26	- **The header is a current view, not a log.** A pass that changes what a page's
27	  most important findings are rewrites the header to match — a superseded
28	  insight leaves it (the correction and its why stay in the body, per below),
29	  and an insight the pass didn't touch stays put. If nothing changed the page's
30	  top-line understanding, the header doesn't move.
31	- **The sink is human-reviewed only.** `product-wiki/product-requirements/` never
32	  changes as a side effect of wiki work or any unattended pass — a wiki finding
33	  that should move a requirement gets a growth-log note (and a repo issue) and
34	  waits for a human. It is the only `product-wiki/` content the rest of the repo may
35	  build on.
36	- **Compile once, refine in place.** Read the target page end to end before
37	  researching; `## Open questions` is the backlog — research what it flags as
38	  open, thin, or dated, and spot-check an existing citation or two per pass.
39	  Never re-derive a claim that's already cited and current.
40	- **Cited, never silently rewritten.** An uncited claim doesn't get written. A
41	  wrong or superseded claim is corrected with a note of why (and its source),
42	  never deleted without trace. Every real change records itself in the page's
43	  growth log and updates the open questions in both directions.
44	- **Seeing a figure in several places is not evidence of who published it.**
45	  Search snippets quote each other, so a number that recurs across five results
46	  is one source repeated, and the firm the snippets name is routinely not the
47	  firm that produced it. When you cannot open the report, attribute the figure to
48	  the publisher a source explicitly names as its **origin**; when sources
49	  disagree about that, say so on the page rather than picking one.
50	- **No fabricated growth.** Most passes find little or nothing; no new citable
51	  material → no edit, no log entry, no PR.
52	- **sample-data and new wikis.** `product-wiki/sample-data/` gains a file only when
53	  a wiki claim needs one to point to — never test fixtures (anything a test
54	  asserts against belongs in engineering's tree). Any folder under `product-wiki/`
55	  outside the two reserved names *is* a wiki (the structural classifier), so
56	  create one only deliberately, seeded with its required sections; automation
57	  refines existing pages, it never invents new ones.
58	- **Review discipline.** Unattended growth always lands as an unmerged PR —
59	  researched claims entering a committed knowledge base need the review gate.
60	  The owner phrase **"grow the product wiki"** runs the worker method
61	  in-session with full web tooling: same rules, same PR discipline.
62

1	# Python
2	
3	Portable, project-agnostic practices for a Python package built around an optional
4	heavy/native dependency (an ML model, a native audio/GPU library, a cloud SDK) that
5	most of the codebase — and the whole test suite — must run without. The theme is one:
6	**keep the importable core dependency-free, and gate every heavy thing behind an
7	optional extra.** What stays here is the architecture judgment that has no
8	false-positive-free static signature; the mechanical shape of the optional import
9	itself (imported lazily, guarded with an install-hint re-raise) is carried by the
10	`python-optional-deps` skill.
11	
12	## Keep the importable core dependency-free; heavy/native deps go in optional extras, not base `dependencies`
13	
14	The core of a package (its logic, storage, CLI, any web/dashboard layer) should import
15	and run — and be **fully testable** — with only the Python standard library. Declare
16	`dependencies = []` (or the genuinely-always-needed minimum) in `[project]`, and put every
17	heavy, native, or ML dependency under a **named `[project.optional-dependencies]` extra**
18	(`pkg[yamnet]`, `pkg[speaker]`, `pkg[dev]`). The test: if a `pip install <pkg>` with no
19	extra can't import the core, a heavy dependency has leaked into the base set — move it
20	to an extra.
21	
22	## Provide a stdlib-only implementation behind the same interface so tests and offline modes need no extra
23	
24	Give the swappable interface a **dependency-free** implementation — a scripted/mock
25	backend built on the standard library alone — alongside the heavy real one; that stdlib
26	backend is what the test suite and any offline/`simulate` mode run on. The heavy backend
27	is then just one more implementation of the interface, selected at runtime, never a hard
28	import the core or the tests depend on. The clean shape is a tiny backend interface plus
29	a `load_default()`/registry that lazy-imports the *selected* backend by name, so the
30	module that wires backends together never imports any of them at load time.
31	
32	## Mark the availability-probe import as a deliberate unused-import suppression
33	
34	An import kept **only** to probe whether an optional stack is present (its name is never
35	used directly — the code just branches on whether the import succeeded) is a real linter
36	false-positive for unused-import (`F401`). Mark that line `# noqa: F401` and record the
37	deliberate suppression, rather than deleting the probe or letting the warning ride.
38

# Python

Portable, project-agnostic practices for a Python package built around an optional
heavy/native dependency (an ML model, a native audio/GPU library, a cloud SDK) that
most of the codebase — and the whole test suite — must run without. The theme is one:
**keep the importable core dependency-free, and gate every heavy thing behind an
optional extra.** What stays here is the architecture judgment that has no
false-positive-free static signature; the mechanical shape of the optional import
itself (imported lazily, guarded with an install-hint re-raise) is carried by the
`python-optional-deps` skill.

## Keep the importable core dependency-free; heavy/native deps go in optional extras, not base `dependencies`

The core of a package (its logic, storage, CLI, any web/dashboard layer) should import
and run — and be **fully testable** — with only the Python standard library. Declare
`dependencies = []` (or the genuinely-always-needed minimum) in `[project]`, and put every
heavy, native, or ML dependency under a **named `[project.optional-dependencies]` extra**
(`pkg[yamnet]`, `pkg[speaker]`, `pkg[dev]`). The test: if a `pip install <pkg>` with no
extra can't import the core, a heavy dependency has leaked into the base set — move it
to an extra.

## Provide a stdlib-only implementation behind the same interface so tests and offline modes need no extra

Give the swappable interface a **dependency-free** implementation — a scripted/mock
backend built on the standard library alone — alongside the heavy real one; that stdlib
backend is what the test suite and any offline/`simulate` mode run on. The heavy backend
is then just one more implementation of the interface, selected at runtime, never a hard
import the core or the tests depend on. The clean shape is a tiny backend interface plus
a `load_default()`/registry that lazy-imports the *selected* backend by name, so the
module that wires backends together never imports any of them at load time.

## Mark the availability-probe import as a deliberate unused-import suppression

An import kept **only** to probe whether an optional stack is present (its name is never
used directly — the code just branches on whether the import succeeded) is a real linter
false-positive for unused-import (`F401`). Mark that line `# noqa: F401` and record the
deliberate suppression, rather than deleting the probe or letting the warning ride.
