1	# Research Project Working Procedures — a portable playbook
2	
3	This document defines **how the owner wants a research project run**, as a
4	**bootstrap to drop into a new research project** from day one. It is written to
5	be project-agnostic: it carries the durable working procedures and none of the
6	subject matter, methods, or results of any particular study.
7	
8	It is aimed at the recurring class of research it is meant for: **run an
9	algorithm over a set of similarly-formatted inputs, score it against
10	user-provided ground truth, and improve the algorithm in repeatable, reviewable
11	iterations.** Image analysis / computer vision is the archetypal case and the
12	examples lean that way, but the workflow, ground-truth discipline,
13	anti-overfitting stance, and session hygiene apply to research work broadly —
14	read "algorithm", "input", and "render" as whatever they mean for your project.
15	
16	Treat it as a **default to adapt, not a contract**. When a new project needs a
17	rule this one doesn't have, add it; when a rule here doesn't fit, say why and
18	drop it. As you work a real project, replace the generic phrasing with that
19	project's concrete specifics (its inputs, metrics, invariants) in *that
20	project's own* docs — keep this bootstrap generic so it stays reusable. The one
21	non-negotiable is the spirit: **show the work visually, prove each change against
22	ground truth, never overfit the learning set, and leave the project resumable.**
23	
24	---
25	
26	## 1. The core loop — iterate on the algorithm, and *show* every step
27	
28	This is the cadence the owner wants, and it is the **deliverable style**, not
29	optional polish. Follow it for every substantive algorithmic change.
30	
31	1. **Reproduce & diagnose — visually, first.** Start from the actual inputs.
32	   Render the current behaviour and *look* at it before theorising. If a
33	   decision hinges on a measurable fact (a colour/intensity split, a threshold,
34	   an over-reach, a distribution), write a **throwaway diagnostic and measure
35	   it** — do not guess.
36	2. **Prototype in the scratchpad.** Build the change as a standalone script
37	   first. Do **not** touch tracked code yet.
38	3. **Show a comparison in the chat.** Surface a rendered **[ original | result ]**
39	   side-by-side — and **[ … | ground truth ]** wherever scoring applies —
40	   directly in the conversation (render it inline, don't just link a path). The
41	   **picture leads**; numbers (accuracy metrics, the target quantity) come
42	   *after* it as confirmation, **never instead of it**.
43	4. **Get a read, then commit to the approach.** Only once the visual result is
44	   right do you wire it into the tracked code. If a call is genuinely ambiguous
45	   or is the owner's to make, ask **one** targeted question; otherwise proceed on
46	   a sensible default and state what you chose.
47	5. **Wire it in fully** — see *Definition of done* (§5).
48	6. **Record it** as a numbered iteration note — what was wrong, what changed, the
49	   metric delta, and **what you tried and rejected** (§5).
50	
51	### Show, don't just tell
52	- Every algorithmic change is presented as a rendered comparison against the
53	  original, and against ground truth when scoring is involved. Prefer a clean,
54	  purpose-built **results figure** over a wall of metrics.
55	- The presentation render is usually **not** the debug overlay. Favour a thin,
56	  semi-transparent style that keeps the underlying data readable (thin lines,
57	  mostly-transparent fills), and give a matched object the **same colour in the
58	  result and the ground-truth panels** so over-/under-reach is obvious at a
59	  glance. Tag objects with small ids that key into the metrics table.
60	- **Never draw an annotation in a colour the underlying signal itself carries.**
61	  A mark in the signal's own colour disappears exactly on the objects it exists
62	  to mark, so the figure looks cleanest where the method is least verified. Pick
63	  the overlay palette against the data's own colours (and keep the choice
64	  guarded, if the render is scripted), not by aesthetic preference.
65	- **Show where the method breaks, not only where it works.** The overlay is a QA
66	  tool before it is a result: point at the misses, the fragmentation, the cases
67	  handled badly, and make each claim explicit and checkable ("this outline is
68	  what I'm counting as an object; that one has no outline — it was missed") so
69	  the owner can disagree with a specific claim rather than a general impression.
70	- **Say which of the numbers you just reported are trustworthy, where you report
71	  them.** Every quantity a project reports sits somewhere on a spectrum from
72	  "measured and validated" to "indicative at best" — a quantity derived from a
73	  low-resolution crop, one still inflated by a known failure mode, a split that
74	  rests on a single threshold. State that boundary *inline, beside the number*,
75	  not in a separate caveats section a reader meets after they have already
76	  written the number down. A number quoted without its caveat is read as
77	  trustworthy.
78	- Throwaway renders and diagnostics live in the scratchpad; only the **final
79	  artifact and the code that regenerates it** get committed.
80	
81	### Interaction cadence
82	Keep the owner in the loop with **pictures**, proactively. Ask a question only
83	when a decision is genuinely theirs or the request is ambiguous — not to confirm
84	work you can verify yourself. When you finish a unit of work, leave it committed
85	and pushed so it can be reviewed or resumed from a fresh session.
86	
87	---
88	
89	## 2. Ground truth — user-provided, annotated, **never invented**
90	
91	- **The owner's annotations are the ground truth.** Every change is validated by
92	  agreement against them, not against your own expectation of the answer.
93	- **Ground truth is annotated, never fabricated.** Do not invent labels to make a
94	  dataset scorable. If a dataset lacks the annotation a given harness needs, it
95	  does not go into that harness (see §9 on validation tiers).
96	- **Separate source-of-truth from generated artifacts.** The hand-annotation is
97	  the source; the machine-usable ground-truth (registered masks, parsed labels,
98	  normalized tables) is **generated from it and regenerated on demand** — never
99	  hand-edited, because the generator overwrites it. To fix ground truth, **fix
100	  the source annotation (or the extraction code) and regenerate**, then re-score.
101	- **Make extraction deterministic and self-checking.** Same annotation → same
102	  derived ground truth. Pin the things a human counted (number of objects,
103	  number of regions) as assertions/tests so a silent extraction regression fails
104	  loudly.
105	- **Auto-detect annotation conventions from the data**, don't hard-code a
106	  per-input flag. When the owner uses more than one annotation scheme over time,
107	  detect which scheme an input uses from the ink/markup itself. Record the
108	  **conventions** (what each colour / mark / region means) in a durable doc; they
109	  are requirements, not incidental.
110	- **Verify the annotation actually parses before trusting a score.** Inspect two
111	  things: did the markup parse into the labels you expected, and did the derived
112	  ground truth land correctly on the raw input (registration / alignment)? Keep
113	  the review overlays.
114	
115	---
116	
117	## 3. Inputs — a small, similarly-formatted learning set
118	
119	- Projects like this begin with a **small learning set of similarly-formatted
120	  inputs** (same modality, same acquisition regime, same annotation convention).
121	  That is a hazard as well as a feature: it is small enough to overfit (§4).
122	- **State the input format explicitly** (dimensions, modality, contrast
123	  convention, expected content per input) so a mismatched new input is diagnosed
124	  fast. Keep a one-line-per-input table.
125	- **Name the primary target regime and what is out of scope.** A different
126	  regime (inverted contrast, far denser or sparser content, a different scale)
127	  is a *transfer* problem, not the main path — treat it as such until explicitly
128	  in scope.
129	- **Scale-awareness is a first-class concern.** An algorithm tuned for one
130	  input scale (e.g. a zoomed view of a few objects) often fails on another
131	  (a wide field of many). Know which regime you are tuned for, and measure the
132	  gap on the other rather than pretending it's covered.
133	
134	---
135	
136	## 4. Do not overfit the learning set
137	
138	These are **hard constraints** — a change that violates one gets reverted even
139	if it improves a metric.
140	
141	- **No single-input special-casing.** Every rule must generalise across the set.
142	  If a fix only helps one input, say so and either generalise it or drop it.
143	  Never key logic on a specific input's identity/filename.
144	- **Keep decision rules free of the very prior you are trying to measure.** If
145	  the project measures quantity *X*, no rule may bake in an assumed value of *X*
146	  (that turns the measurement into an assumption). Prefer rules expressed in
147	  terms the input **measures for itself** over fixed constants.
148	- **Prefer scale-free rules over pixel/absolute constants.** Where a constant is
149	  unavoidably tied to the current data's scale/resolution, **isolate and label
150	  it** as scale-dependent so it is the first thing revisited on new-scale data.
151	- **Name the hard constraint the task cannot trade away**, and tune to it first —
152	  some projects have a metric whose cost dominates all others; hold it at its
153	  required level before optimising the softer metrics underneath it. Make it
154	  explicit so a later tuning pass doesn't quietly trade it away.
155	- **Keep a registry of domain assumptions, each with a failure mode.** Choices
156	  that encode a prior about the *subject or the instrument* (not pure
157	  processing) are named, located in the code with an inline tag, and given an
158	  explicit "how it fails on mismatched data" note. When a new input looks wrong,
159	  the first diagnostic is *"which assumption did this input break?"*. Flag the
160	  thinly-supported ones (e.g. calibrated on a single example) honestly.
161	- **Guard the wins with regression tests.** An input the owner has blessed as
162	  "very good" must not silently regress when you tune for another. Pin its score.
163	
164	---
165	
166	## 5. Repeatable improvement iterations — the numbered notes, and *definition of done*
167	
168	Each accepted change is recorded as a **numbered iteration note** (pick a short
169	tag and stick to it, e.g. `R1, R2, …`) in a running method-narrative doc, so
170	**the next session does not re-derive what this one already learned.**
171	
172	An iteration note captures:
173	- **What was wrong** (the observed failure, ideally with the diagnostic that
174	  showed it).
175	- **What changed** (the rule/parameter and why, in scale-free terms where
176	  possible).
177	- **The metric delta** — before/after, per input, on the real scoring harness.
178	- **What you tried and rejected, and why** — this is what stops the next session
179	  (or the next model) from walking back into the same dead end.
180	
181	### A metric's definition is part of its identity
182	
183	Write down what each reported metric actually counts, and treat **re-defining
184	one as the owner's call, never a tuning step**. A definition change is uniquely
185	silent: the column keeps its name and its units, so every number ever recorded
186	under it *looks* comparable while the quantity underneath has moved. When a
187	definition does change, the history is **re-measured, never re-labelled** — rerun
188	the old inputs under the new definition, or mark the old numbers as belonging to
189	the old one. Carrying both definitions' numbers in one series under one name is
190	the failure this rule exists to prevent.
191	
192	### A raw measurement is comparable only inside one calibration
193	
194	When each input carries its own scale (a per-image conversion factor, a per-run
195	sampling rate, a per-source unit), a raw absolute quantity means something
196	different in every input. **Aggregate and compare only normalized quantities** —
197	a density, a ratio, a per-unit rate — never the raw number, and never a mean
198	spanning two sources that differ in more than scale (a different instrument,
199	subject or protocol changes *what* is measured, not just how much of it fits in
200	frame). Group the rollup by source and say what the grouping is for.
201	
202	The conversion factor is a **measurement of that input**, not a constant: read it
203	off the input itself, never infer it from a stated setting or borrow it from a
204	neighbour. It lives in exactly one place in the code — a second copy is a second
205	calibration, and whichever copy a given script happens to read wins silently. An
206	input offering nothing to measure the factor from is **not** quietly dropped:
207	mark it uncalibrated *with the reason*, report only its scale-free quantities,
208	and leave it visible as a known gap.
209	
210	### Definition of done for an accepted change
211	- **Source updated — never the generated artifacts.** (Regenerate them.)
212	- **Artifacts regenerated** with the committed generators.
213	- **Tests green**, and the **scoring deltas reported** (per input, per metric).
214	- **Committed with a clear message and pushed**, so the work is reviewable and
215	  resumable from a fresh session / another machine.
216	- **Learnings cached**: the iteration note above, plus a pointer/update in the
217	  session warm-up doc or the relevant reference doc **if the map or procedure
218	  changed**.
219	
220	---
221	
222	## 6. Research phases, and spikes vs the main path
223	
224	- **Separate work into explicit phases**, each with a bounded deliverable, and
225	  say which phase a piece of work belongs to. Defer the hard/advanced piece
226	  explicitly rather than half-building it — e.g. get an intermediate output
227	  trusted before building the final quantity that depends on it.
228	- **Distinguish research spikes from the maintained pipeline.** Exploratory
229	  scripts are worth keeping for reference, but the repo map must make clear what
230	  "the pipeline" actually is versus what was an older spike, so a new session
231	  doesn't mistake a dead branch for the main path.
232	- **Keep a "known open items" / deferred list** so the boundary between "done",
233	  "deferred by choice", and "not yet attempted" is never ambiguous.
234	
235	---
236	
237	## 7. Reading & summarizing source articles
238	
239	When a paper, tool, or reference method matters to the project:
240	
241	- **Write a self-contained notes file so the source never has to be re-read.**
242	  Capture everything algorithmically relevant: the exact method/pipeline and its
243	  parameters, the definitions and formulae, calibration details, and **sanity-check
244	  values** you can validate your own outputs against.
245	- **Capture the method that exists only inside a figure.** Part of a source's
246	  actual procedure is often drawn rather than written — a panel's inset, an
247	  annotated overlay, a legend. Extract and describe it in the notes; a summary
248	  built from the prose alone silently omits it, and the omission is invisible
249	  until someone re-opens the source.
250	- **Write down what the source *fails* to say**, as an explicit gap list — the
251	  parameters, thresholds and units it never states. Recording an absence is what
252	  stops the next reader re-opening the source to hunt for something that was
253	  never in it. The intake is done when the notes make the original redundant, and
254	  a stated gap is part of that.
255	- **Explicitly record where your approach diverges from the reference and why.**
256	- **State what you deliberately omitted** (material not relevant to the
257	  algorithm — e.g. procedural/experimental setup detail, incidental statistics,
258	  acknowledgements) and that you cross-checked against the full text — so a later
259	  reader trusts the summary is complete for its purpose.
260	- Note that upload paths for source PDFs are **session-specific and won't
261	  persist**; the notes file is the durable artifact, not the upload.
262	
263	---
264	
265	## 8. Extracting images — samples vs illustrations
266	
267	- **Samples** are inputs you will run the algorithm on; **illustrations** are
268	  figures that explain a method or a definition. Keep the two roles distinct and
269	  store extracted figures alongside the notes that reference them.
270	- **Render documents with a library, not an assumed system binary.** The
271	  environment often lacks common tools (e.g. a PDF rasterizer such as poppler /
272	  `pdftoppm`); use an in-process library instead. Locate embedded raster images
273	  and render just the region you need, at a zoom high enough to read fine
274	  annotation, with a little padding to catch ink drawn outside the frame.
275	- **Verify identity when an extracted image should match an existing input**
276	  (e.g. an annotated crop over an original) by an exact pixel diff — so you know
277	  an annotation set is a labelling of the *same* data, not a new input.
278	
279	---
280	
281	## 9. Fetching more sample data from the outside
282	
283	- **Grow the corpus from public sources that match the input regime.** Curate and
284	  **rank candidates by fit** = modality match × ground-truth availability × ease
285	  of access, and record licence and provenance for each.
286	- **Make ingestion a committed, repeatable fetch script**, not a manual download,
287	  so anyone can reproduce the corpus.
288	- **Respect the two validation tiers — and don't mix them:**
289	  - **Full ground truth** (per-item annotations) → scores the *algorithm's
290	    detailed output* (overlap / detection) on the real harness.
291	  - **Aggregate label only** (a published summary number, no per-item
292	    annotation) → validates the *summary quantity* the project reports, and
293	    nothing finer.
294	  Wiring an aggregate-only dataset into the detailed-overlap harness would force
295	  you to **fabricate annotations**, which violates §2. Keep a separate,
296	  mask-free validation path for those sets.
297	- **External data is rarely drop-in.** Expect a scale/regime gap (§3) and
298	  *measure* it with the appropriate tier rather than assuming the corpus is
299	  covered.
300	
301	---
302	
303	## 10. Environment limitations — stay lightweight
304	
305	- **A fresh container has nothing installed.** Assume dependencies must be
306	  installed each session, and keep the dependency set **small and lightweight** —
307	  favour a compact set of core libraries over heavy frameworks (e.g. large ML
308	  stacks) that are slow to install and awkward to run anywhere.
309	- **When a heavy or learned approach is genuinely the right tool, treat it as a
310	  gated, isolated route** (documented, opt-in, scoped to the cases that need it)
311	  rather than a new baseline dependency — and prove the lightweight route is
312	  exhausted first.
313	- **Route around missing system binaries with libraries** (see §8). Document the
314	  exact install lines and any "install ad hoc, not in requirements" tools in the
315	  warm-up doc.
316	
317	---
318	
319	## 11. Getting — and evaluating — algorithm ideas from the owner
320	
321	The owner will suggest algorithms and directions to try next. Treat these as
322	first-class experiments:
323	
324	- **Take the suggestion seriously even when the project has declared a direction
325	  "exhausted."** A suggestion may belong to a *different family* than everything
326	  tried so far, which is exactly when it can break a wall the previous family
327	  couldn't.
328	- **Evaluate it the same way as any change**: diagnose the wall it targets, build
329	  the evidence that the wall is real (or isn't), prototype, and show a comparison.
330	- **Beat the naive baseline, or drop it.** A more sophisticated or signal-driven
331	  method is only worth adopting if it *measurably* out-scores the simple/uniform
332	  baseline — sophistication is not accuracy when the guiding signal is noisy or
333	  penetrates the structure unevenly. Keep the roles of a signal distinct, too: a
334	  feature that is excellent for *visualising or validating* a structure can be
335	  wrong for *defining* it — gating the output directly on such a signal can erode
336	  the very structure you are measuring.
337	- **Document the outcome fully**, including the routes that hit a wall and *why*
338	  (name the specific trade-off or signal that defeated them). If the idea needs
339	  capabilities the environment won't allow (§10), record the concrete route to
340	  try when that changes, so the thread is resumable rather than lost.
341	- **Complementary routes are not competitors.** Two methods can attack the same
342	  problem from different angles; keep both documented and say how they relate.
343	
344	---
345	
346	## 12. Record cross-domain applicability **out-of-band**
347	
348	When a sub-step of the algorithm plausibly applies to **another problem** beyond
349	the current task, record it as a **short pointer in a dedicated side document** —
350	a direction worth attention, not a validated claim. **Keep this speculation out
351	of the algorithm itself**: code and inline comments stay strictly about the task
352	at hand and its stated assumptions. Add an entry whenever you build or
353	substantially change a sub-step.
354	
355	---
356	
357	## 13. Continuity across sessions
358	
359	The owner works across many sessions and machines. Every session should end in a
360	**resumable** state.
361	
362	- **Commit and push** finished units of work; leave the project runnable from a
363	  clean checkout.
364	- **Maintain a session warm-up doc** (the "read this first" map): what the project
365	  is, how to run it, where the tuned parameters and the deep rationale live, and
366	  the current numbers. It should let a new session skip re-reading the whole
367	  codebase.
368	- **Maintain a continuation guide**: where things stand, exact run commands, the
369	  tuned parameters and *why they exist*, and the open items. Keep the headline
370	  metrics current in it.
371	- **When the owner asks for a different way to do something, capture the new way
372	  durably — don't just do it this once.** A correction to *how* work is done (how
373	  results are shown, what command to run, a naming/format convention, a step to
374	  always take or skip) is a standing preference, not a one-off. Fold it into the
375	  warm-up doc — or a reference doc linked from it. Prefer editing the doc that
376	  already owns that topic over adding a stray note; if the change contradicts
377	  what's written, replace it and say what changed. The test: *could a fresh
378	  session, with only the warm-up doc, reproduce this new behaviour?* If not, it
379	  isn't captured yet.
380	- Follow the repo's **branch/commit/PR conventions**: develop on the named
381	  branch, commit with clear messages, push; don't open a PR unless asked.
382	
383	---
384	
385	## 14. Reviving a prior session to **enhance this document** (not to continue the research)
386	
387	Some of the owner's process preferences live only in the **dialogue of earlier
388	Claude Code (web) sessions**, not in any committed file. If the owner revives
389	such a session and points it at this playbook, here is the instruction for that
390	revived session:
391	
392	> **Your job in this revived session is to mine our conversation for *process and
393	> working-style preferences*, and fold them into this playbook — NOT to continue
394	> the research task itself.**
395	> Re-read the whole dialogue and extract only the durable, project-agnostic
396	> signal about *how the owner wants research run*: how they want results shown;
397	> what they praised or rejected about the workflow (not just the algorithm);
398	> ground-truth and annotation conventions; anti-overfitting rules they insisted
399	> on; how they want articles summarized, images extracted, and external data
400	> fetched; environment constraints they flagged; and how they hand off algorithm
401	> ideas. For each item, strip out anything specific to this project's subject
402	> matter and generalise it to the class of "run a CV/analysis algorithm over
403	> similarly-formatted inputs, scored against user ground truth, improved in
404	> reviewable iterations." Then propose additions/edits to the relevant numbered
405	> section above (merge, don't duplicate; keep the principle-first phrasing). Show
406	> the owner a diff of what you'd add and confirm the wording before committing.
407	> **Do not run or modify the research pipeline.** If a preference contradicts what
408	> is already written here, surface the conflict for the owner rather than silently
409	> overwriting.
410	
411	To make revival productive, when the owner asks for it they should say **which
412	session(s)** to revive (a link or a description) and, if possible, what topic the
413	process discussion centred on — so the revived session knows where in the
414	transcript to look.
415

# Research Project Working Procedures — a portable playbook

This document defines **how the owner wants a research project run**, as a
**bootstrap to drop into a new research project** from day one. It is written to
be project-agnostic: it carries the durable working procedures and none of the
subject matter, methods, or results of any particular study.

It is aimed at the recurring class of research it is meant for: **run an
algorithm over a set of similarly-formatted inputs, score it against
user-provided ground truth, and improve the algorithm in repeatable, reviewable
iterations.** Image analysis / computer vision is the archetypal case and the
examples lean that way, but the workflow, ground-truth discipline,
anti-overfitting stance, and session hygiene apply to research work broadly —
read "algorithm", "input", and "render" as whatever they mean for your project.

Treat it as a **default to adapt, not a contract**. When a new project needs a
rule this one doesn't have, add it; when a rule here doesn't fit, say why and
drop it. As you work a real project, replace the generic phrasing with that
project's concrete specifics (its inputs, metrics, invariants) in *that
project's own* docs — keep this bootstrap generic so it stays reusable. The one
non-negotiable is the spirit: **show the work visually, prove each change against
ground truth, never overfit the learning set, and leave the project resumable.**

---

## 1. The core loop — iterate on the algorithm, and *show* every step

This is the cadence the owner wants, and it is the **deliverable style**, not
optional polish. Follow it for every substantive algorithmic change.

1. **Reproduce & diagnose — visually, first.** Start from the actual inputs.
   Render the current behaviour and *look* at it before theorising. If a
   decision hinges on a measurable fact (a colour/intensity split, a threshold,
   an over-reach, a distribution), write a **throwaway diagnostic and measure
   it** — do not guess.
2. **Prototype in the scratchpad.** Build the change as a standalone script
   first. Do **not** touch tracked code yet.
3. **Show a comparison in the chat.** Surface a rendered **[ original | result ]**
   side-by-side — and **[ … | ground truth ]** wherever scoring applies —
   directly in the conversation (render it inline, don't just link a path). The
   **picture leads**; numbers (accuracy metrics, the target quantity) come
   *after* it as confirmation, **never instead of it**.
4. **Get a read, then commit to the approach.** Only once the visual result is
   right do you wire it into the tracked code. If a call is genuinely ambiguous
   or is the owner's to make, ask **one** targeted question; otherwise proceed on
   a sensible default and state what you chose.
5. **Wire it in fully** — see *Definition of done* (§5).
6. **Record it** as a numbered iteration note — what was wrong, what changed, the
   metric delta, and **what you tried and rejected** (§5).

### Show, don't just tell
- Every algorithmic change is presented as a rendered comparison against the
  original, and against ground truth when scoring is involved. Prefer a clean,
  purpose-built **results figure** over a wall of metrics.
- The presentation render is usually **not** the debug overlay. Favour a thin,
  semi-transparent style that keeps the underlying data readable (thin lines,
  mostly-transparent fills), and give a matched object the **same colour in the
  result and the ground-truth panels** so over-/under-reach is obvious at a
  glance. Tag objects with small ids that key into the metrics table.
- **Never draw an annotation in a colour the underlying signal itself carries.**
  A mark in the signal's own colour disappears exactly on the objects it exists
  to mark, so the figure looks cleanest where the method is least verified. Pick
  the overlay palette against the data's own colours (and keep the choice
  guarded, if the render is scripted), not by aesthetic preference.
- **Show where the method breaks, not only where it works.** The overlay is a QA
  tool before it is a result: point at the misses, the fragmentation, the cases
  handled badly, and make each claim explicit and checkable ("this outline is
  what I'm counting as an object; that one has no outline — it was missed") so
  the owner can disagree with a specific claim rather than a general impression.
- **Say which of the numbers you just reported are trustworthy, where you report
  them.** Every quantity a project reports sits somewhere on a spectrum from
  "measured and validated" to "indicative at best" — a quantity derived from a
  low-resolution crop, one still inflated by a known failure mode, a split that
  rests on a single threshold. State that boundary *inline, beside the number*,
  not in a separate caveats section a reader meets after they have already
  written the number down. A number quoted without its caveat is read as
  trustworthy.
- Throwaway renders and diagnostics live in the scratchpad; only the **final
  artifact and the code that regenerates it** get committed.

### Interaction cadence
Keep the owner in the loop with **pictures**, proactively. Ask a question only
when a decision is genuinely theirs or the request is ambiguous — not to confirm
work you can verify yourself. When you finish a unit of work, leave it committed
and pushed so it can be reviewed or resumed from a fresh session.

---

## 2. Ground truth — user-provided, annotated, **never invented**

- **The owner's annotations are the ground truth.** Every change is validated by
  agreement against them, not against your own expectation of the answer.
- **Ground truth is annotated, never fabricated.** Do not invent labels to make a
  dataset scorable. If a dataset lacks the annotation a given harness needs, it
  does not go into that harness (see §9 on validation tiers).
- **Separate source-of-truth from generated artifacts.** The hand-annotation is
  the source; the machine-usable ground-truth (registered masks, parsed labels,
  normalized tables) is **generated from it and regenerated on demand** — never
  hand-edited, because the generator overwrites it. To fix ground truth, **fix
  the source annotation (or the extraction code) and regenerate**, then re-score.
- **Make extraction deterministic and self-checking.** Same annotation → same
  derived ground truth. Pin the things a human counted (number of objects,
  number of regions) as assertions/tests so a silent extraction regression fails
  loudly.
- **Auto-detect annotation conventions from the data**, don't hard-code a
  per-input flag. When the owner uses more than one annotation scheme over time,
  detect which scheme an input uses from the ink/markup itself. Record the
  **conventions** (what each colour / mark / region means) in a durable doc; they
  are requirements, not incidental.
- **Verify the annotation actually parses before trusting a score.** Inspect two
  things: did the markup parse into the labels you expected, and did the derived
  ground truth land correctly on the raw input (registration / alignment)? Keep
  the review overlays.

---

## 3. Inputs — a small, similarly-formatted learning set

  inputs** (same modality, same acquisition regime, same annotation convention).
  That is a hazard as well as a feature: it is small enough to overfit (§4).

  convention, expected content per input) so a mismatched new input is diagnosed

  in scope.

  input scale (e.g. a zoomed view of a few objects) often fails on another
  (a wide field of many). Know which regime you are tuned for, and measure the
  gap on the other rather than pretending it's covered.

---

- **No single-input special-casing.** Every rule must generalise across the set.
  If a fix only helps one input, say so and either generalise it or drop it.

  terms the input **measures for itself** over fixed constants.

  unavoidably tied to the current data's scale/resolution, **isolate and label
  it** as scale-dependent so it is the first thing revisited on new-scale data.

  some projects have a metric whose cost dominates all others; hold it at its
  required level before optimising the softer metrics underneath it. Make it
  explicit so a later tuning pass doesn't quietly trade it away.
- **Keep a registry of domain assumptions, each with a failure mode.** Choices
  that encode a prior about the *subject or the instrument* (not pure
  processing) are named, located in the code with an inline tag, and given an
  explicit "how it fails on mismatched data" note. When a new input looks wrong,
  the first diagnostic is *"which assumption did this input break?"*. Flag the
  thinly-supported ones (e.g. calibrated on a single example) honestly.
- **Guard the wins with regression tests.** An input the owner has blessed as
  "very good" must not silently regress when you tune for another. Pin its score.

---

## 5. Repeatable improvement iterations — the numbered notes, and *definition of done*

Each accepted change is recorded as a **numbered iteration note** (pick a short
tag and stick to it, e.g. `R1, R2, …`) in a running method-narrative doc, so
**the next session does not re-derive what this one already learned.**

An iteration note captures:
- **What was wrong** (the observed failure, ideally with the diagnostic that
  showed it).
- **What changed** (the rule/parameter and why, in scale-free terms where
  possible).
- **The metric delta** — before/after, per input, on the real scoring harness.
- **What you tried and rejected, and why** — this is what stops the next session
  (or the next model) from walking back into the same dead end.

### A metric's definition is part of its identity

Write down what each reported metric actually counts, and treat **re-defining
one as the owner's call, never a tuning step**. A definition change is uniquely
silent: the column keeps its name and its units, so every number ever recorded
under it *looks* comparable while the quantity underneath has moved. When a
definition does change, the history is **re-measured, never re-labelled** — rerun
the old inputs under the new definition, or mark the old numbers as belonging to
the old one. Carrying both definitions' numbers in one series under one name is
the failure this rule exists to prevent.

### A raw measurement is comparable only inside one calibration

When each input carries its own scale (a per-image conversion factor, a per-run
sampling rate, a per-source unit), a raw absolute quantity means something
different in every input. **Aggregate and compare only normalized quantities** —

spanning two sources that differ in more than scale (a different instrument,

frame). Group the rollup by source and say what the grouping is for.

The conversion factor is a **measurement of that input**, not a constant: read it
off the input itself, never infer it from a stated setting or borrow it from a
neighbour. It lives in exactly one place in the code — a second copy is a second
calibration, and whichever copy a given script happens to read wins silently. An
input offering nothing to measure the factor from is **not** quietly dropped:
mark it uncalibrated *with the reason*, report only its scale-free quantities,
and leave it visible as a known gap.

### Definition of done for an accepted change
- **Source updated — never the generated artifacts.** (Regenerate them.)
- **Artifacts regenerated** with the committed generators.
- **Tests green**, and the **scoring deltas reported** (per input, per metric).
- **Committed with a clear message and pushed**, so the work is reviewable and
  resumable from a fresh session / another machine.
- **Learnings cached**: the iteration note above, plus a pointer/update in the
  session warm-up doc or the relevant reference doc **if the map or procedure
  changed**.

---

## 6. Research phases, and spikes vs the main path

- **Separate work into explicit phases**, each with a bounded deliverable, and
  say which phase a piece of work belongs to. Defer the hard/advanced piece
  explicitly rather than half-building it — e.g. get an intermediate output
  trusted before building the final quantity that depends on it.
- **Distinguish research spikes from the maintained pipeline.** Exploratory
  scripts are worth keeping for reference, but the repo map must make clear what
  "the pipeline" actually is versus what was an older spike, so a new session
  doesn't mistake a dead branch for the main path.
- **Keep a "known open items" / deferred list** so the boundary between "done",
  "deferred by choice", and "not yet attempted" is never ambiguous.

---

## 7. Reading & summarizing source articles

When a paper, tool, or reference method matters to the project:

- **Write a self-contained notes file so the source never has to be re-read.**
  Capture everything algorithmically relevant: the exact method/pipeline and its
  parameters, the definitions and formulae, calibration details, and **sanity-check
  values** you can validate your own outputs against.
- **Capture the method that exists only inside a figure.** Part of a source's
  actual procedure is often drawn rather than written — a panel's inset, an
  annotated overlay, a legend. Extract and describe it in the notes; a summary
  built from the prose alone silently omits it, and the omission is invisible
  until someone re-opens the source.
- **Write down what the source *fails* to say**, as an explicit gap list — the
  parameters, thresholds and units it never states. Recording an absence is what
  stops the next reader re-opening the source to hunt for something that was
  never in it. The intake is done when the notes make the original redundant, and
  a stated gap is part of that.
- **Explicitly record where your approach diverges from the reference and why.**
- **State what you deliberately omitted** (material not relevant to the
  algorithm — e.g. procedural/experimental setup detail, incidental statistics,
  acknowledgements) and that you cross-checked against the full text — so a later
  reader trusts the summary is complete for its purpose.
- Note that upload paths for source PDFs are **session-specific and won't
  persist**; the notes file is the durable artifact, not the upload.

---

## 8. Extracting images — samples vs illustrations

- **Samples** are inputs you will run the algorithm on; **illustrations** are
  figures that explain a method or a definition. Keep the two roles distinct and
  store extracted figures alongside the notes that reference them.
- **Render documents with a library, not an assumed system binary.** The
  environment often lacks common tools (e.g. a PDF rasterizer such as poppler /
  `pdftoppm`); use an in-process library instead. Locate embedded raster images
  and render just the region you need, at a zoom high enough to read fine
  annotation, with a little padding to catch ink drawn outside the frame.
- **Verify identity when an extracted image should match an existing input**
  (e.g. an annotated crop over an original) by an exact pixel diff — so you know
  an annotation set is a labelling of the *same* data, not a new input.

---

## 9. Fetching more sample data from the outside

- **Grow the corpus from public sources that match the input regime.** Curate and
  **rank candidates by fit** = modality match × ground-truth availability × ease
  of access, and record licence and provenance for each.
- **Make ingestion a committed, repeatable fetch script**, not a manual download,
  so anyone can reproduce the corpus.
- **Respect the two validation tiers — and don't mix them:**
  - **Full ground truth** (per-item annotations) → scores the *algorithm's
    detailed output* (overlap / detection) on the real harness.
  - **Aggregate label only** (a published summary number, no per-item
    annotation) → validates the *summary quantity* the project reports, and
    nothing finer.
  Wiring an aggregate-only dataset into the detailed-overlap harness would force
  you to **fabricate annotations**, which violates §2. Keep a separate,
  mask-free validation path for those sets.
- **External data is rarely drop-in.** Expect a scale/regime gap (§3) and
  *measure* it with the appropriate tier rather than assuming the corpus is
  covered.

---

## 10. Environment limitations — stay lightweight

- **A fresh container has nothing installed.** Assume dependencies must be
  installed each session, and keep the dependency set **small and lightweight** —
  favour a compact set of core libraries over heavy frameworks (e.g. large ML
  stacks) that are slow to install and awkward to run anywhere.
- **When a heavy or learned approach is genuinely the right tool, treat it as a
  gated, isolated route** (documented, opt-in, scoped to the cases that need it)
  rather than a new baseline dependency — and prove the lightweight route is
  exhausted first.
- **Route around missing system binaries with libraries** (see §8). Document the
  exact install lines and any "install ad hoc, not in requirements" tools in the
  warm-up doc.

---

## 11. Getting — and evaluating — algorithm ideas from the owner

The owner will suggest algorithms and directions to try next. Treat these as
first-class experiments:

- **Take the suggestion seriously even when the project has declared a direction
  "exhausted."** A suggestion may belong to a *different family* than everything
  tried so far, which is exactly when it can break a wall the previous family
  couldn't.
- **Evaluate it the same way as any change**: diagnose the wall it targets, build
  the evidence that the wall is real (or isn't), prototype, and show a comparison.
- **Beat the naive baseline, or drop it.** A more sophisticated or signal-driven
  method is only worth adopting if it *measurably* out-scores the simple/uniform
  baseline — sophistication is not accuracy when the guiding signal is noisy or
  penetrates the structure unevenly. Keep the roles of a signal distinct, too: a
  feature that is excellent for *visualising or validating* a structure can be
  wrong for *defining* it — gating the output directly on such a signal can erode
  the very structure you are measuring.
- **Document the outcome fully**, including the routes that hit a wall and *why*
  (name the specific trade-off or signal that defeated them). If the idea needs
  capabilities the environment won't allow (§10), record the concrete route to
  try when that changes, so the thread is resumable rather than lost.
- **Complementary routes are not competitors.** Two methods can attack the same
  problem from different angles; keep both documented and say how they relate.

---

## 12. Record cross-domain applicability **out-of-band**

When a sub-step of the algorithm plausibly applies to **another problem** beyond
the current task, record it as a **short pointer in a dedicated side document** —
a direction worth attention, not a validated claim. **Keep this speculation out
of the algorithm itself**: code and inline comments stay strictly about the task
at hand and its stated assumptions. Add an entry whenever you build or
substantially change a sub-step.

---

## 13. Continuity across sessions

The owner works across many sessions and machines. Every session should end in a
**resumable** state.

- **Commit and push** finished units of work; leave the project runnable from a
  clean checkout.
- **Maintain a session warm-up doc** (the "read this first" map): what the project
  is, how to run it, where the tuned parameters and the deep rationale live, and
  the current numbers. It should let a new session skip re-reading the whole
  codebase.
- **Maintain a continuation guide**: where things stand, exact run commands, the
  tuned parameters and *why they exist*, and the open items. Keep the headline
  metrics current in it.
- **When the owner asks for a different way to do something, capture the new way
  durably — don't just do it this once.** A correction to *how* work is done (how
  results are shown, what command to run, a naming/format convention, a step to
  always take or skip) is a standing preference, not a one-off. Fold it into the
  warm-up doc — or a reference doc linked from it. Prefer editing the doc that
  already owns that topic over adding a stray note; if the change contradicts
  what's written, replace it and say what changed. The test: *could a fresh
  session, with only the warm-up doc, reproduce this new behaviour?* If not, it
  isn't captured yet.
- Follow the repo's **branch/commit/PR conventions**: develop on the named
  branch, commit with clear messages, push; don't open a PR unless asked.

---

## 14. Reviving a prior session to **enhance this document** (not to continue the research)

Some of the owner's process preferences live only in the **dialogue of earlier
Claude Code (web) sessions**, not in any committed file. If the owner revives
such a session and points it at this playbook, here is the instruction for that
revived session:

> **Your job in this revived session is to mine our conversation for *process and
> working-style preferences*, and fold them into this playbook — NOT to continue
> the research task itself.**
> Re-read the whole dialogue and extract only the durable, project-agnostic
> signal about *how the owner wants research run*: how they want results shown;
> what they praised or rejected about the workflow (not just the algorithm);
> ground-truth and annotation conventions; anti-overfitting rules they insisted
> on; how they want articles summarized, images extracted, and external data
> fetched; environment constraints they flagged; and how they hand off algorithm
> ideas. For each item, strip out anything specific to this project's subject
> matter and generalise it to the class of "run a CV/analysis algorithm over
> similarly-formatted inputs, scored against user ground truth, improved in
> reviewable iterations." Then propose additions/edits to the relevant numbered
> section above (merge, don't duplicate; keep the principle-first phrasing). Show
> the owner a diff of what you'd add and confirm the wording before committing.
> **Do not run or modify the research pipeline.** If a preference contradicts what
> is already written here, surface the conflict for the owner rather than silently
> overwriting.

1	# Spec-Driven Product Working Procedures — a portable playbook
2	
3	This document defines **how the owner wants a spec-driven product project run**, as a **bootstrap to
4	drop into a new project of this class** from day one. The class: **build and ship a small end-user
5	product against an executable specification — every requirement is a numbered leaf claimed by exactly
6	one executable proof of the right kind, expected results are owned by the owner, and releases cut
7	automatically while `main` stays green.** The archetype is a UI-centric product (a browser-extension
8	panel, a small web or mobile app) and the examples lean that way, but the discipline applies wherever
9	observable behavior can be specified leaf by leaf — read "surface", "render", and "server" as whatever
10	they mean for your project.
11	
12	It is written to be project-agnostic: it carries the durable working procedures and none of the
13	product, stack, or harness specifics of any particular project. Those live elsewhere — platform
14	gotchas in the project's technology packs, release mechanics in its release pack or release doc, and
15	the concrete spec, harness, and commands in the project's own docs. General test-trust practices
16	(see-it-fail, snapshot hygiene, the re-baselining approval procedure, capture-artifact-first) are
17	corpus canon in the writing-tests skill; this pack assumes them and adds the class's development loop
18	on top.
19	
20	Treat it as a **default to adapt, not a contract**: when a rule here doesn't fit, say why and drop it;
21	when the project needs a rule this document lacks, add it in the project's own docs first. The
22	non-negotiable is the spirit: **the spec is executable, the expecteds belong to the owner, the real
23	code produces every actual, and the product ships on green.**
24	
25	---
26	
27	## 1. The executable spec is the backbone
28	
29	- **One numbered requirements document states what the product must do**, leaf by leaf: what each
30	  surface must render, how it must behave, the exact copy and semantics it must carry. Not prose
31	  aspirations — specific, testable statements.
32	- **Keep the spec's boundary crisp: a leaf is what the harness can assert.** The feature-level story —
33	  what the product does and why — lives in the product's prose docs; the spec holds the specific,
34	  testable statements (exact strings, placement, semantics). A statement no kind can prove isn't a
35	  leaf yet: it stays prose, or it's the trigger to add the kind that can prove it.
36	- **Every leaf carries a stable id.** Add new requirements under new numbers; never renumber or reuse
37	  a retired one — the ids are what cases, commits, and review discussion key on.
38	- **Doc-first, red by default.** Adding a leaf with no executable proof fails the build until a case
39	  claims it.
40	- **The spec drives the tests, never the other way around.** A behavior change starts by editing the
41	  leaf, watching the gate go red, then changing product and proof to match. A test changed without its
42	  leaf — or a leaf reworded to match what the code happens to do — inverts the authority.
43	
44	## 2. Every leaf ⇄ exactly one proof, of the right kind
45	
46	- **Enforce the bijection with a committed coverage gate**: each leaf claimed by exactly one case,
47	  each case claiming exactly one leaf, and every discovered kind of case actually executed by a
48	  runner. The gate is part of the project's own suite.
49	- **A *kind* is one way a requirement can be asserted** — a rendered-state snapshot, a driven gesture,
50	  a pure rule, a boundary-enforced rule. Route each leaf to the kind that can actually observe what it
51	  asserts. Keep kinds **extensible** — adding one is a self-contained drop.
52	- **A kind may be a singleton.** "The product loads in the real environment" is a perfectly good leaf
53	  whose mechanism is one end-to-end case; the kind names the *way of asserting*, not a population of
54	  cases.
55	- **Give each kind's runner a named lane, and keep the default lane fast and deterministic.** Heavy
56	  real-environment kinds gate the merge from CI without slowing the inner loop; their trust rules
57	  (twice-green before merging, self-diagnosing on failure) are canon in the writing-tests skill.
58	- **Actuals come from the real code.** Whatever the kind, the proof drives the shipped entry points
59	  under a faithful harness — never a parallel re-implementation of what production "should" do (the
60	  writing-tests skill owns the general rule).
61	
62	## 3. Expected results are owner-owned
63	
64	- **The committed expecteds are the owner's approval record of the product.** A case's success
65	  criterion encodes what the owner accepted.
66	- **The contract takes two honest shapes.** *Artifact-expected* (a committed render, an exact-values
67	  file): the owner approves a committed file — an agent may **propose** the expected for a brand-new
68	  leaf, but never modifies a committed one to make a failing case pass. *Coded-expected* (an
69	  assertion, a `verify()`): the expected **is** the assertion — keep it outside the write surface of
70	  whatever writes the product code, so passing by weakening the check isn't even expressible.
71	- **On a mismatch, surface actual vs. expected (and the diff) and ask.** The re-baselining procedure —
72	  diff shown, owner approves, only then re-baseline — is canon in the writing-tests skill, and it
73	  applies uniformly: to a moved render, a changed values file, and a failing assertion alike.
74	- **Expected changes ride the normal review flow** — they land in the diff like code, so the owner
75	  approves the product change and its new expected together, once.
76	
77	## 4. State a requirement once; prove it at every boundary that enforces it
78	
79	- **A product rule with more than one enforcing tier gets sibling leaves under one statement** — e.g.
80	  "only signed-in users can post": the surface's half (the client sends credentials) and the
81	  boundary's half (the server rejects an unauthenticated write) are separate proofs of one
82	  requirement.
83	- **The proof lives where the rule is actually enforced.** A surface-side test of a server-enforced
84	  rule proves only that the client cooperates, not that the boundary holds; if the real enforcement is
85	  the backend, a leaf must exist there, exercised against the real handler.
86	
87	## 5. A supported-targets matrix is spec, not folklore
88	
89	- **When part of the product's value is breadth over external targets** — supported sites, file
90	  formats, providers, locales — each supported target is its own leaf, so dropping a target is a
91	  visible spec change, not a silent regression.
92	- **Prove each target against a committed, real sample of it** (a captured page, a genuine file), with
93	  the owner-reviewed exact-values expectation committed beside it — capture the sample first and read
94	  the expecteds off the committed bytes (canon in the writing-tests skill). A hand-invented sample
95	  proves support for a target the world doesn't actually serve.
96	- **Adding a target is a documented, repeatable flow** that lands the new leaf, its real sample, and
97	  its reviewed expected together.
98	
99	## 6. Green means "claimed", not "fully verified" — track the gap honestly
100	
101	- **Say what the harness cannot reach, naming the exact boundary of each stub.** A faithful harness is
102	  still a model of the platform; the honest sentence pattern is "this proof confirms our code *asks*
103	  for the action, not that the platform *performs* it". Put that statement where readers of the spec
104	  will see it — a banner on the requirements doc, linking the issue that tracks closing the gap —
105	  rather than in a test README footnote.
106	- **Deliberate gaps are marked at the leaf and committed, never remembered.** A leaf that can't be
107	  faithfully verified yet stays in the spec, visibly provisional (a loud "to be decided" marker, and a
108	  pointer to whatever covers it meanwhile), and is listed in a committed allowlist the coverage gate
109	  checks — the allowlist is the burn-down list, shrunk deliberately. Prefer a real validation; reach
110	  for the marker only for a genuinely undecided edge case or a not-yet-wired harness.
111	
112	## 7. The owner reviews the product surface, not the internals
113	
114	- **Embed regenerated renders of the real states in the spec itself** — the requirements document
115	  doubles as a gallery of what the product actually shows, generated from the shipped code, so
116	  approving the spec *is* approving the product's appearance.
117	- **Regenerate, never hand-edit.** The gallery is derived output of a committed generator; fixing it
118	  means fixing the source (or the generator) and regenerating.
119	- **The deterministic golden-image method this leans on is canon in the writing-tests skill** —
120	  matching the render engine to the surface (a bit-exact rasterizer for inline-styled/SVG surfaces, a
121	  headless browser for pages that use grid/vars/emoji/form-widgets), bundled fonts, capturing a
122	  host-page surface with styles inlined, and a drift gate on the embedded gallery.
123	
124	## 8. Ship automatically while `main` stays green
125	
126	- **`main` is releasable at all times, and automation does the releasing** — a release (and, where
127	  the platform has one, store publication) cuts from `main` on its own cadence without a human build
128	  step. Keeping `main` green *is* the release gate: a red `main` is a shipping outage, fixed before
129	  new work.
130	- **The version users see moves deliberately.** Automation may patch-bump to ship, but a meaningful
131	  version change is a decision made on `main`, not a side effect. The concrete release contract —
132	  workflows, artifacts, store procedures — belongs to the project's release pack or release doc, not
133	  here.

1	# web-scraping — taking data from a site you don't own
2	
3	The facet: a project whose input is another organisation's website, reached without a
4	contract. There is no support channel, no changelog and no SLA, so every rule below is about
5	**reducing what you have to re-learn** — from the site, from the network, and from your own
6	pipeline — when it changes underneath you.
7	
8	A default to adapt, not a contract. Language-agnostic: "fetch", "parse" and "normalize" mean
9	whatever they mean on your stack.
10	
11	## Finding the data surface
12	
13	- **Adding a source, or deciding what to parse** — scraping rendered markup is the **last**
14	  resort. Prefer, in order: the hydration blob a server-rendered app embeds in the page, then
15	  the JSON/GraphQL endpoint a single-page app fetches its rows from, and only then the markup
16	  — where you prefer the page's self-describing metadata (JSON-LD, `og:` tags) over element
17	  positions, because metadata survives a redesign and `.results > div:nth-child(2)` does not.
18	  Finding that surface on a new site is a one-off reconnaissance job with its own procedure,
19	  the [`map-a-data-source`](skills/map-a-data-source/SKILL.md) skill.
20	
21	- **A rendered-snapshot expectation shifting after a re-record** — rendered output is **not
22	  deterministic**, so treat the shift the way you'd treat a markup change: re-review it, don't
23	  assume a regression.
24	
25	- **Learning something non-obvious by probing the service** — write it down in a reference doc
26	  beside the scripts: endpoints, auth, the field surface, the enum values. Keep it complete
27	  enough that **nothing needs to re-probe the live service to answer a question**. The
28	  expensive part of this work is the knowledge rather than the code, and re-probing is slow,
29	  rate-limited, sometimes blocked, and occasionally the thing that gets you banned.
30	
31	## Fetching
32	
33	- **Writing the fetch itself** — browser-like headers, a randomized delay between requests, and
34	  exponential backoff on retry. Route **all** outbound page/API fetching through a single
35	  module, so swapping the vendor, the proxy or the credential is one edit with one place to
36	  test.
37	
38	- **Deciding whether to retry a failed request** — retry only what can improve. A gateway or
39	  proxy failure (408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504) is worth another attempt; any other 4xx is about
40	  your request and will answer the same way forever.
41	
42	- **Porting a fetch to a language-level HTTP client** — carry the retry policy across the
43	  rewrite. `curl --retry` covers exactly that status set and the port silently drops all of it,
44	  so the first transient 500 the old command would have ridden out kills the run.
45	
46	- **Setting the retry budget** — attempts times per-attempt timeout, plus the waits, must fit
47	  inside whatever hard limit kills the process, and the backoff should be injectable so tests
48	  exercise the retry path without sleeping through it.
49	
50	- **One item in a batch failing to fetch** — record and continue. Log the reason per item and
51	  emit a report; one unfetchable item should not abandon the batch.
52	
53	- **A sandbox refusing the target host** — an agent sandbox is commonly **bot-blocked**, and its
54	  egress proxy may refuse the host outright. That refusal is policy: **do not route around it**,
55	  not with a local fetch and not with an ad-hoc workflow spun up to reach the host. Give the
56	  fetch one sanctioned home — a scheduled job or workflow on a runner, with the credential in
57	  repository secrets — and let sessions read the committed raw records instead.
58	
59	- **A fetch that works on your machine and fails from CI** — a 403/400 or a CAPTCHA wall from a
60	  runner or a sandbox is usually the *datacenter IP* being blocked, not the headers, so tuning
61	  them is wasted work. **Reaching a commercial rendering proxy** is the standard answer: a
62	  residential lane clears the IP block, and these services usually execute JavaScript too, so a
63	  single-page app records real content. Ask it to render, and give it a wait-for-selector when
64	  the content you want arrives late. A target that stays blocked even through the proxy is
65	  un-cacheable: say so and stop, rather than hunting for another route.
66	
67	- **Needing many items from a service with no list endpoint** — no bulk endpoint is not the same
68	  as no bulk request. GraphQL lets one document alias the same field many times, and many REST
69	  APIs accept a multi-id parameter. The cap is usually undocumented, so **halve a rejected batch
70	  and retry** — that keeps batch size a throughput knob and never an accuracy one.
71	
72	- **A fetch that cannot produce a page at all** — a bot wall, a dead URL, an empty render is a
73	  dead end, not a pipeline failure: mark the item for a human and **exit successfully**. Failing
74	  the run converges on the same human signal while also implying the pipeline broke, when in
75	  fact it correctly declined. The rest of the batch should still land.
76	
77	## Reading what came back
78	
79	- **Deciding whether a fetch succeeded** — a 200 is not success. An anti-bot interstitial arrives
80	  as a normal-looking 200 (or a 403/503) whose body is a challenge page, and caching it stores
81	  garbage that looks like data. Match the known markers in the first few KB and report it as a
82	  distinct failure reason.
83	
84	- **Getting an empty body back** — nothing rendered. Treat it as a failure of that fetch rather
85	  than as an empty result, and don't retry it: a successful-but-empty response will keep being
86	  successful and empty.
87	
88	- **Choosing which field to read** — prefer the authoritative status enum over the summarizing
89	  convenience boolean, which is routinely wrong: an item can report "not sold out" while its
90	  status says there is nothing left to sell. Take the enum's legal values from the service's own
91	  options endpoint rather than from what you happened to see.
92	
93	- **Filtering rows by a status** — deny-list the bad statuses, don't allow-list the good ones,
94	  and log the set actually observed. A new status then defaults to usable and shows up in your
95	  logs, instead of silently dropping rows.
96	
97	- **Reading a numeric field** — numbers may arrive as strings. Parse; don't assume the JSON type.
98	
99	- **Reducing a set to its "cheapest" or "first"** — that value can be a special case rather than
100	  a value. Filter to what the field means before you reduce over it: a zero-priced accessibility
101	  companion band makes the cheapest ticket for every show free.
102	
103	## Normalizing what you read
104	
105	- **Converting an instant to the domain's local time** — instants usually arrive in UTC while
106	  your domain thinks in local wall-clock. Do the conversion in one function at the ingestion
107	  boundary and have everything downstream speak local time. Slicing digits out of the string
108	  files everything an hour off during daylight saving, and **the result looks completely
109	  plausible** — nothing throws, nothing is empty, the data is simply wrong. Because the failure
110	  is silent, keep a **known-answer probe**: an item whose correct value you know independently
111	  (something named after its own time, a figure published elsewhere), checked after every fresh
112	  pull. "Exactly once" cuts both ways — a stage downstream of the boundary that parses,
113	  re-offsets or re-reads a stored value as UTC is the same bug from the other end.
114	
115	- **Taking a "now"** — read it in the domain's zone rather than off the device clock. A reviewer
116	  in the same zone as the developer cannot see the difference, which is how a device clock
117	  survives review.
118	
119	- **Parsing a value whose format is ambiguous** — read it by what the page declares, centrally;
120	  never per-source, never guessed. A numeric slash date whose parts are both ≤ 12 (`05/07/2026`)
121	  has no intrinsic answer, so resolve it from a *positive* signal the document gives you (an
122	  explicit region in `<html lang>` or `og:locale`, a non-English language) and keep the default
123	  when the signal is absent or region-less, rather than inferring one from the host or the
124	  venue. Put that resolution in one helper the whole pipeline threads, so a new source cannot
125	  invent its own reading. A trailing `Z` or `+00:00` is *serialization*, not a claim about the
126	  subject's zone: it neither supplies the zone nor vetoes deriving one from what the page says
127	  about the place.
128	
129	- **Changing the conversion** — it is a **full-snapshot change**. Committed derived data is
130	  generator output, so the fix isn't done until the raw record is re-run through the new
131	  conversion and every downstream artifact regenerated. Expect the boundary to move records
132	  between partitions — items at the end of a day land in the next one, and may fall outside the
133	  range your day-partitioned files cover — and check that rather than reading it as data loss.
134	
135	- **Emitting a value your pipeline hasn't reached yet** — missing is its own state: *unknown*,
136	  never folded into *free*, *empty* or *false*. Sources keep adding rows after your last full
137	  pass, so gaps are normal and permanent. Carry unknown through the whole stack — omit the key
138	  rather than emitting a default — and let each consumer render it as its own thing.
139	
140	## What lands on disk, and when it refreshes
141	
142	- **Deciding what a fetch writes to disk** — two forms, separated deliberately. The fetched
143	  artifact (page HTML, raw response pages) is a **cache**: git-ignore it, since it is large,
144	  regenerable, and not what you reason about. The extracted raw record — the site's own object,
145	  before any of your normalization — is **committed**, and is the durable source of truth. That
146	  split buys three things at once: re-deriving your normalized output becomes an **offline**
147	  operation, so a parser change costs no requests; the committed record doubles as the fixture
148	  for a self-test of the transform that needs no network; and a field you didn't parse this
149	  month is still there next month, because you kept the whole object rather than the subset you
150	  needed at the time.
151	
152	- **Re-running a fetch that already ran** — **fetch only what's missing**, with an explicit flag
153	  to force a refresh, so repeat runs are a no-op. Note what "resumable" is measured against: the
154	  file on disk. On a CI runner that file is durable only once the job's commit step pushes it,
155	  so a resumable script still loses everything if the runner itself dies. Chunk the work if that
156	  matters.
157	
158	- **Scheduling the refresh** — give each field its own pass on the clock it actually moves on.
159	  The single biggest cost saving in a scraper is noticing that some fields are fixed once
160	  published, some gain rows daily and some move hourly: re-fetching everything on the fastest
161	  clock re-learns a static field nightly, thousands of requests for the same answer, and it is
162	  the part of your traffic most likely to get you blocked.
163	
164	- **Generating the artifacts downstream of the stored data** — make them a **pure function of
165	  the stored master**: refresh writes to the master, and everything else regenerates from it.
166	  Files whose inputs didn't change come back byte-identical and never enter the commit, so the
167	  diff of a scheduled run is exactly what actually moved.
168

  pull. "Exactly once" cuts both ways — a stage downstream of the boundary that parses,
  re-offsets or re-reads a stored value as UTC is the same bug from the other end.

- **Taking a "now"** — read it in the domain's zone rather than off the device clock. A reviewer
  in the same zone as the developer cannot see the difference, which is how a device clock
  survives review.

- **Parsing a value whose format is ambiguous** — read it by what the page declares, centrally;
  never per-source, never guessed. A numeric slash date whose parts are both ≤ 12 (`05/07/2026`)
  has no intrinsic answer, so resolve it from a *positive* signal the document gives you (an
  explicit region in `<html lang>` or `og:locale`, a non-English language) and keep the default
  when the signal is absent or region-less, rather than inferring one from the host or the
  venue. Put that resolution in one helper the whole pipeline threads, so a new source cannot
  invent its own reading. A trailing `Z` or `+00:00` is *serialization*, not a claim about the
  subject's zone: it neither supplies the zone nor vetoes deriving one from what the page says
  about the place.

- **Changing the conversion** — it is a **full-snapshot change**. Committed derived data is
  generator output, so the fix isn't done until the raw record is re-run through the new
  conversion and every downstream artifact regenerated. Expect the boundary to move records
  between partitions — items at the end of a day land in the next one, and may fall outside the
  range your day-partitioned files cover — and check that rather than reading it as data loss.

- **Emitting a value your pipeline hasn't reached yet** — missing is its own state: *unknown*,
  never folded into *free*, *empty* or *false*. Sources keep adding rows after your last full
  pass, so gaps are normal and permanent. Carry unknown through the whole stack — omit the key
  rather than emitting a default — and let each consumer render it as its own thing.

## What lands on disk, and when it refreshes

- **Deciding what a fetch writes to disk** — two forms, separated deliberately. The fetched
  artifact (page HTML, raw response pages) is a **cache**: git-ignore it, since it is large,
  regenerable, and not what you reason about. The extracted raw record — the site's own object,
  before any of your normalization — is **committed**, and is the durable source of truth. That
  split buys three things at once: re-deriving your normalized output becomes an **offline**
  operation, so a parser change costs no requests; the committed record doubles as the fixture
  for a self-test of the transform that needs no network; and a field you didn't parse this
  month is still there next month, because you kept the whole object rather than the subset you
  needed at the time.

- **Re-running a fetch that already ran** — **fetch only what's missing**, with an explicit flag
  to force a refresh, so repeat runs are a no-op. Note what "resumable" is measured against: the
  file on disk. On a CI runner that file is durable only once the job's commit step pushes it,
  so a resumable script still loses everything if the runner itself dies. Chunk the work if that
  matters.

- **Scheduling the refresh** — give each field its own pass on the clock it actually moves on.
  The single biggest cost saving in a scraper is noticing that some fields are fixed once
  published, some gain rows daily and some move hourly: re-fetching everything on the fastest
  clock re-learns a static field nightly, thousands of requests for the same answer, and it is
  the part of your traffic most likely to get you blocked.

- **Generating the artifacts downstream of the stored data** — make them a **pure function of
  the stored master**: refresh writes to the master, and everything else regenerates from it.
  Files whose inputs didn't change come back byte-identical and never enter the commit, so the
  diff of a scheduled run is exactly what actually moved.

14	## Speech-to-text (`webkitSpeechRecognition` / Web Speech API)
15	
16	- **The recognizer owns its own microphone capture — you cannot hand it
17	  `getUserMedia` audio constraints.** `echoCancellation` / `noiseSuppression` /
18	  `autoGainControl` are `getUserMedia` *microphone* constraints, and the recognizer
19	  exposes no hook to set them on its internal stream (Chrome applies its default
20	  echo cancellation there regardless). To *warm* the device with a known processing
21	  state — and to read back whether echo cancellation actually engaged — run a
22	  separate preflight `getUserMedia({ audio: {…} })` capture and stop its tracks.
23	  (`suppressLocalAudioPlayback` /
24	  `restrictOwnAudio` are `getDisplayMedia` *screen-capture* constraints and have no
25	  bearing on a mic — don't reach for them here.)
26	- **Read the whole n-best list, not just alternative `[0]`.** Set
27	  `maxAlternatives` > 1 and iterate `result[0..length]` for `{ transcript,
28	  confidence }`; the ranked alternatives are exactly where homophone / near-miss
29	  recovery lives.
30	- **`onresult`, `onend`, and `onerror` all fire — settle the cycle exactly once.**
31	  Guard a `settled` flag: interim results arrive before the final one, a cycle can
32	  end with no result at all (treat `onend`-without-result as `no-speech`), and an
33	  error and an end can both arrive.
34	- **With `interimResults` off, engines omit `isFinal` — treat a result as final
35	  unless `isFinal === false`.** Don't test `if (result.isFinal)` (it's `undefined`
36	  on those engines and you'll drop every result); test `result.isFinal !== false`.
37	- **The classic recognizer streams audio to a cloud service (Google's) — plan for
38	  it.** A `network` error means "offline / service unreachable", and audio leaves
39	  the machine. On-device recognition is opt-in and capability-gated: probe
40	  `SpeechRecognition.available({ langs, processLocally: true }) === 'available'`
41	  once and cache it, set `recognizer.processLocally = true`, and **never trigger a
42	  language-pack download** (only `'available'` counts, not `'downloadable'`). When

52	  `service-not-allowed` → permission-denied, plus `no-speech`, `network`,

54	  *self-inflicted* stop (you called `recognizer.abort()`), so the caller should
55	  ignore it rather than surface it as a failure.

58	  endpoint; a timer that fires after a pause discards the half-heard input and
59	  reopens a fresh cycle (preventing "heart heart" doubles when the user repeats
60	  themselves). Set the threshold **well above a natural mid-command thinking
61	  pause** — a tight window (~1.2 s) cuts real commands; a wider one (~1.8 s) keeps
62	  only the genuine missed-endpoint case.

100	  punctuation cue matters (a question's rising tone), speak the cue in words
